doc_level_notes: Overarching argument: SNA is a general, transferable method. Its value to Paul's systems lies in converting heterogeneous source data (legal citations, lobbying reports, policy memos, tweets, campaign donations, committee rosters) into weighted, directed or multi-layer graphs, then running community detection (Louvain) and centrality.
Recurring problem 1: two-mode or bipartite structures must become one-mode graphs before path-finding can run (Kim and Kunisky; Mason and Mucha raise the same display question).
Recurring problem 2: temporal weighting is missing in several works (Fink; Malaterre on office closeness).
Recurring problem 3: directionality, causal ordering and information availability affect validity (Haythornthwaite; Mason and Mucha chicken-or-egg; Gaynor on leadership insulation).
Recurring problem 4: sign of ties is undefined for negative interactions (Fink).

Research questions implied by the annotations: who the champions are for rival or allied industries and how committed they are (Kim); how congestion shows up in the data (Kim); whether hidden communities of interest can be inferred from text (Malaterre); whether partisan alignment drives committee selection (Mason and Mucha); whether campaign donations bind caucuses and whether leadership insulates members (Gaynor).

Stated gaps: Ardekani does not track lobbying, consulting, co-sponsorship or money; Gaynor does not cover committee action, voting or co-sponsorship; Haythornthwaite is thin on graph construction; Kim and Kunisky lack a bipartite-to-graph route; Mason and Mucha lack a clear way to show members and committees on one graph; Fink lacks sign and temporal rules; Malaterre needs a temporal element and possibly domain-specific topic models.
Priority tags: Haythornthwaite is Priority Medium, Theory; Malaterre and Lareau is Priority Very High, Foundational. These are Paul's own labels and are carried into the takeaways.
Methodological leads Paul flags for later work: centrality types need more research (Ardekani); the Viral Centrality Algorithm needs testing for compute time and as a Monte Carlo analogue (Fink).

Newman and Casey Warmbrand too; Kim and Kunisky's citation spells the co-author Dmitriy Kunisky, but the annotation spells it Dimitriy Kuinsky; Malaterre's citation has markup damage ('Data &amp*; Policy'); 'Louvian' is misspelled in two places in the annotations.

works.title: A hypergraph analysis of the European Commission lobby network
works.summary:
Azaiez and Mandel model five years of disclosed European Commission meetings (Dec 2019 to Nov 2024) as a hypergraph. Each meeting is one hyperedge joining officials and stakeholders, giving 5,717 nodes and 18,561 meetings. The hypergraph is one connected component and splits into Commissioner-centred silos (modularity 0.700). Most meetings are one-on-one. The rare large meetings hold the network together: edge betweenness correlates 0.74 with meeting size.

Among stakeholders only, a size- and degree-preserving null model shows a rich club at every degree k. The full network cannot be tested the same way, because it has no official-only meetings to compare against. A hypercore decomposition puts companies and trade associations in the core of the full network and NGOs in the core of the stakeholder-only network. In a standardized OLS over 1,178 companies (R2 0.398), hypercoreness rises with lobbying FTE (0.464) and assets (0.253). The authors say this is association only, with reverse causation possible.

The most portable result for Paul is methodological. Projecting meetings onto pairwise cliques inflates nodes that attend a few large meetings. Coreness on the clique projection agrees only weakly with coreness on the hypergraph; within each framework the two measures correlate at 0.93 and 0.79. Melange builds two clique-style projections of group events: cosponsor rosters, and staffer payroll containers. The cosponsor network already discounts big bills by 1/sqrt(C). The staffer co-tenure operator has an open owner ruling on container-size normalization, and the paper's inflation finding is direct evidence for that ruling. It also helps explain the recorded r = 0.87 between staffer degree and office size.

The paper also says centrality measures embeddedness, not influence, and that resources drive it. This fits the system's retirement of cosponsor centrality from the Influence pillar and D-025's wording rule. The paper's own Discussion slips into "access and influence" language, which must not carry over. The paper's edges come from a register that names both parties to each contact. US LD-2 filings do not, so this design cannot be reproduced with LDA data (D-021).
works.question: Does a highly interconnected core of actors dominate the European Commission lobbying network (p.2)? What determines company centrality in that network (p.2, p.8), and do stakeholder categories (companies, trade associations, NGOs) differ in their core position (p.6-7)?
works.method: Hypergraph construction from meeting co-attendance. Global structure: degree shares by stakeholder category, modularity (Louvain-type clustering, SI 8.4), edge-size and betweenness analysis, simpliciality (Landry et al. 2024) and edge entropy. Core-periphery: generalized normalized rich-club coefficient for hypergraphs, rho(k) = phi(k)/phi_rand(k), with phi_rand from six hypergraph configuration null models (Chodrow 2020), sampled by Metropolis-Hastings edge-swap rewiring (p.14-15). Hypercore decomposition (k,m) and hypercoreness centrality R(i) (Mancastroppa 2023, p.16). Core(r) composition by category for r where Core(r) is 10% to 1% of nodes (p.6-7). Comparison of hypercoreness with coreness on clique-expansion graphs (Pearson correlations, p.16-17). Regression: OLS of company hypercoreness on log FTE lobbying staff, log assets, binary levels of interest (European, global, national), EU head-office dummy, and NACE sector dummies (baseline C Manufacturing); coefficients standardized; skewed variables log-transformed; categories grouped; outliers removed (p.8-9, p.17-18).

findings.finding: Global structure: the hypergraph is one connected component with heavy-tailed degrees; companies and groups account for 34.58% of stakeholder degree, trade and business associations 25.35%, NGOs 23.08%, all others 17.00%.
Meeting size and connectivity: most meetings are one-on-one, but large meetings are rare and key to connectivity. Edge betweenness correlates strongly with edge size.
findings.numbers: correlation 0.74 between edge betweenness and edge size

findings.finding: Siloed organization: the full network has strong community structure centred on individual Commissioners, so departments rarely share meetings.
findings.numbers: modularity 0.700

findings.finding: Stakeholder-only network is less connected. Its largest component holds 43.32% of nodes, with many small components. Meetings are homogeneous by stakeholder type. Meetings are more nested than random chance.
findings.numbers: largest component 43.32%; three simpliciality scores higher in the data than in size- and degree-preserving random hypergraphs (values in SI Fig. 14)

findings.finding: Rich-club among stakeholders: on the stakeholder-only hypergraph, rho(k) > 1 at all k under the stakeholder-only null models. The authors read this as persistent rich-club behaviour among stakeholders.
findings.numbers: rho(k) > 1 for all k

findings.finding: Full-network rich-club is not testable as stated: the full H lacks EC-only edges, which biases rho downward against null models that contain them. Under the hybrid null, the stakeholder rich-club is qualitatively present but less salient.
findings.numbers: rho < 1 for k > 10 under null models (1)-(2); hybrid null (3)-(4) quantitatively weaker

related.why: Bacik measures the US LDA (LobbyView) lobbying network over 1999-2023; Azaiez measures the EC meetings register 2019-2024. Together they contrast a disclosure regime whose filings do not record meetings with named members (LDA) with one that names both parties to each meeting (EC register).

Porter projects the two-mode member-by-committee network onto a one-mode committee graph (normalised interlocks). Azaiez shows that projecting group structures to pairwise graphs changes core rankings relative to a hypergraph treatment.

Sotoudeh builds a cosponsorship network (a projection of bill rosters) and finds an outcome-based influence measure predicts House bill passage better than eigenvector, closeness and strength centrality. Azaiez gives a general reason projected centrality can mislead.

Azaiez's reading of NGO core presence in the stakeholder-only network cites Hanegraaff and Pritoni (2019) on coalitions as a sign of weakness (p.10); Pritoni 2025 reviews that coalition literature and tests the 'relative weakness' hypothesis.

Battaglini and Patacchini model PAC allocation by legislators' Bonacich centrality; Azaiez finds interest-group resources associated with the groups' own centrality (associational, reverse causation acknowledged). The system's kb_benchmark is diagnostic only.

works.title: Identifying hidden coalitions in the US House of Representatives by optimally partitioning signed networks based on generalized balance
works.summary:
Aref and Neal build signed House networks from co-sponsorship for 19 sessions (1981-2017, about 445 members each). They use an SDSM backbone, so an edge is positive when a pair co-sponsors significantly more than chance and negative when significantly less (alpha .01, Holm). They then solve two binary linear programs to global optimality: the minimum frustrated edges for a fixed k, and the smallest k that reaches the overall minimum. In every session the party split leaves more frustrated edges than the optimal 2-partition, and that leaves more than the optimal 3-partition. k*min runs from 3 to 7, but gains past k=3 are small. The third coalition is small (4 to 69 members) and its ideology shifts from session to session. It is the most effective coalition in most sessions on the CEL LES. It also has an unusual sign pattern: 21.18 negative ties per positive tie, against 2.68 for the two main blocs, and 25.6% of its negative ties go to co-partisans, against 8.44%. All of this is descriptive. There are no controls and no causal design.

What this means for the system as built: `fec/network/signed_coalitions.py` cites this paper but works on a different graph. It partitions the LLM-valenced member-mention layer, which mixes House and Senate and is 83% positive, using a heuristic local search capped at k=3. Its stored artifact (2026-07-19) shows a single main bloc plus a 14-member splinter at k=2. At k=3 the third cluster has one member, and frustration barely moves (1040.79 to 1039.79 weighted). So the system has not reproduced the paper's finding and has not tested it. The paper's real substrate, a signed co-sponsorship backbone, is not built in the live code. The June vote backbone threw away exactly the negative ties that define the third coalition. The CEL LES data is already on disk, so a House-only reproduction is cheap. The finding should stay UNVERIFIED until that reproduction runs.
works.question: (1) Can globally optimal partitions of a signed network into k mutually divisive, internally cohesive clusters (generalized balance / k-clusterability) be computed for realistic social networks? (2) What is the smallest k that minimizes frustrated edges? (3) Does partitioning US House legislators by their signed collaboration and opposition ties fit the chamber better than partitioning by party, and what does the resulting structure say about legislative effectiveness?
works.method:
Two binary linear programs, solved to global optimality with Gurobi 9.1 on a 32-core Windows Server VM (p.4). Eq. (1), the k-partition model: binary x_ic assigns node i to cluster c, and f_ij flags frustrated edges. The objective is the minimum frustrated edges for fixed k, C_k(G). Constraints are O(n^2). Eq. (2), a reformulation of the correlation clustering / clique partitioning model (Demaine et al. 2006) for non-complete graphs: binary y_ij marks same-cluster pairs, with constraints over connected triads T. It returns C(G), the minimum over all k, and k*min. Constraints are O(n^3). Signed networks come from the Stochastic Degree Sequence Model in the R backbone package (v1.5.0), with family-wise error alpha = 0.01 via Holm-Bonferroni (p.7-8). Comparison: frustrated-edge counts for party partitions vs optimal k-partitions for k = 2..7. Then coalition mean legislative effectiveness and median ideology, with 95% CI bands (Fig. 4). Analysis is descriptive and per session, with no regression reported.</method>

works.title: Similarity-based link prediction in social networks using latent relationships between the users
works.summary:
Zareie and Sakellariou propose DICN, a link-prediction score that multiplies a direct term (1 + common neighbours) by an indirect term (1 + the Pearson correlation of two nodes' neighbourhood vectors, which include second-order neighbours). They motivate it with two observations. First, between 3.1% (UAL) and 53.7% (YST) of existing edges join nodes that share no common neighbour. Second, at the same common-neighbour count, linked and unlinked pairs overlap heavily. They test it on nine small, static, unweighted, undirected networks, holding out 20% of edges at random over 15 repeats and scoring with AUC only. DICN has the highest AUC in 8 of 9 networks. The margins over the best baseline range from about 0.01 (INF, HAM) to about 0.055 (NSC), and DICN loses on UAL. It also wins in 5 of 9 networks on pairs with no common neighbour, and in 5 of 9 on pairs with equal common-neighbour counts, where it is clearly worst on UAL (0.568 vs 0.792). No variances or significance tests are reported. Weighted and directed graphs are left to future work.

For Melange, the paper is a candidate source of dyadic features, not evidence about influence. The sharpest use is in the ridge-logistic cosponsor forecaster. Its only pair-level network signal is the direct prior sponsor-to-member affinity count. Every other network term describes a single node (degree, eigenvector), so common-neighbour and second-order similarity between the sponsor and the candidate are missing. The press HCoI layer already uses the correlation-of-profiles idea through Malaterre, but it uses correlation alone, without the direct term. Any DICN-style score in this system is a heuristic similarity output, not closeness, access or introduction probability (D-025). It stays UNVERIFIED until it is reproduced under the forecaster's own temporal split (DE-062).
works.question: Can similarity scores for link prediction that go beyond common first-order neighbours (through a latent relationship captured by the correlation of second-order neighbourhood profiles) predict missing or future links more accurately than eight established similarity baselines?
works.method: Similarity-based link prediction. For each node i, a neighbourhood vector N_i (Eq. 10, p.6) has entries d_i at the node itself, CN_iz for second-order neighbours, CN_iz + 1 for first-order neighbours, and 0 otherwise. The union set UN_ij (Eq. 11) is the set of indices where either vector is positive. The indirect similarity Corr_ij is the Pearson correlation of N_i and N_j over UN_ij (Eqs. 12-13). The DICN score is DICN_ij = (1 + CN_ij)(1 + Corr_ij) (Eq. 14, p.7). Algorithm 1 (p.6) gives the pseudo-code. Evaluation: edges are randomly split into a training set (beta = 80% by default, 50-90% swept in Exp. 2) and a test set; the process is repeated 15 times and averaged. AUC (Eq. 15, pp.7-8) is computed by comparing every test edge with every non-existing pair, counting ties as 0.5. Eight baselines were implemented in Java: CN, PA, JC, HPI, CNDP, NCC, CCPA and SHOPI.

findings.finding: Common neighbours miss many links: a share of existing edges have no common neighbour. Shares range from 3.1% (UAL) to 53.7% (YST).

Existing and non-existing links overlap heavily at the same common-neighbour count, so the count alone separates them poorly. Fig. 2 shows the overlap, with roughly an even split near 8 common neighbours for INF, EML and YST.
findings.numbers: around 8 common neighbours (INF, EML, YST); no tabulated values in the text

findings.finding: Proposed DICN score combines direct similarity (common neighbours) with indirect similarity (Pearson correlation of second-order neighbourhood vectors). Worked examples: Corr_25 about -0.74 gives DICN_25 = 0.26; Corr_38 about 0.32 and Corr_31 about 0.01 for the Fig. 3 pairs.
findings.numbers: DICN_25 = 0.26; Corr_25 about -0.74; Corr_38 about 0.32; Corr_31 about 0.01

findings.finding: Experiment 1 (beta = 80): DICN has the highest AUC in eight of nine networks. In UAL it is close to the best but not the best.
findings.numbers: DICN vs best other: KRT 0.7654 vs 0.7336 (CNDP); DLN 0.7943 vs 0.7570 (CCPA); UAL 0.9367 vs 0.9416 (NCC); NSC 0.9747 vs 0.9195 (CNDP); INF 0.9553 vs 0.9483 (CCPA); EML 0.8932 vs 0.8729 (SHOPI); YST 0.8278 vs 0.7892 (CCPA); HAM 0.9725 vs 0.9617 (CCPA); KHN 0.8839 vs 0.8509 (SHOPI)

findings.finding: Experiment 2 (beta swept 50-90): DICN is consistently best for beta of 70 or higher in seven of nine networks. It is not always best at small training fractions, which the authors attribute to weaker detectable correlation.
findings.numbers: seven of nine networks at beta >= 70; Fig. 5 values not given in text

findings.finding: Experiment 3 (Hypothesis 1, pairs with no common neighbours and degree > 1): among PA, CCPA, SHOPI and DICN, DICN is best in five networks and close to the best in the other four.
findings.numbers: DICN best: KRT 0.8319, NSC 0.8471, EML 0.7595, HAM 0.7831, KHN 0.8001. Others: DLN 0.7028 vs CCPA 0.7211; UAL 0.7979 vs SHOPI 0.8091; INF 0.7979 vs SHOPI 0.8404; YST 0.7609 vs PA 0.7755

Zareie also uses Pearson correlation, but on structural neighbourhood vectors, and multiplies it by a direct common-neighbour term. The overlap is technique-level, not the same method.
Signed (positive and negative) link prediction covers the negative-tie question for the reference layer, which Zareie's unsigned similarity does not address.
Predicts negative links from positive links and interaction content (Epinions, Slashdot), which fills the signed-tie gap this method leaves open.
Builds undirected, weighted, time-decayed House cosponsorship graphs. A DICN-style dyadic feature would have to be adapted to that weighted setting, which Zareie leaves to future work.
Same authors. A narrative survey of behaviour-aware influence-maximization methods, the downstream use of tie estimates in cascade models.

works.title: Universal multilayer network exploration by random walk with restart
works.summary:
Baptista, Gonzalez and Baudot (2022) extend random walk with restart (RWR, a seed-personalized PageRank) to "universal" multilayer networks. These combine any number of multiplex networks, where the same nodes appear on several layers, linked by bipartite networks. They build one column-normalized supra-heterogeneous transition matrix with separate dials for layer jumps (delta), jumps between networks (lambda) and restart allocation (eta, tau). The method ships as the MultiXrank Python package.

They test it with leave-one-out ranking (LOOCV) and link prediction on two examples: a gene/drug/disease network and a three-country airport network. In the biological network, adding the drug multiplex did not help. The cause was low bipartite overlap: only 23% of genes and 5% of diseases are shared across the bipartite links. In the airport network, adding the German layer did help, because overlap there is high. Adding artificial transit nodes raised performance, and gradually randomizing those links lowered it again. Across 125 parameter sets, top-ranked outputs were stable in parts of the biological network and very unstable in the airport network.

Three parts of Paul's system are close to this. The staffer network's layer-balanced PageRank already runs a random walk over several layers: each node splits its transition mass equally across its active layers, and teleport is balanced across entity kinds. However, it checks sensitivity only on damping (0.70/0.85/0.95), never on how mass is split across layers. The Congress multilayer builder merges the cosponsor, engagement, HCoI, social and co-appearance layers into a single edge weight, so it has no layer-jump parameter. No held-out test checks whether each added layer improves anything; the only per-layer evidence is null neighbour co-movement on the cosponsor and HCoI layers. The paper's main lesson for this system is to test whether each layer earns its place, and how much its links overlap with the base graph, before treating more layers as more signal. It gives no evidence about legislatures, lobbying or social ties.
works.question: Can random walk with restart (RWR) be generalized to explore any combination of multiplex, monoplex and bipartite networks (a "universal multilayer network"), and how do added network layers and bipartite links change prediction performance and the stability of outputs to input parameters?
works.method: Formal: derivation of RWR on universal multilayer networks (Eqs 1-16), with the normalization generalized from Li and Patra 2010 and Valdeolivas et al. 2018 to N multiplex networks. Implemented as the Python package MultiXrank (optimized, pip installable; complexity analysis in Supplementary Note 2). Evaluation: (a) Leave-One-Out Cross-Validation (LOOCV): each known gene-disease association left out in turn, remaining associations used as seeds, rank of left-out gene recorded and CDF of ranks plotted (p.4-5, Fig. 3a-b). (b) Link Prediction (LP): a gene-disease edge removed and its gene ranked with the disease as seed (p.6, Figs S11, S14). (c) Controls: artificially added transit drug nodes linking gene-disease pairs (1, 2 or 5 per association; Fig 3c-d) and progressive random rewiring of the enhanced bipartite networks (p.5-6). (d) Parameter-space exploration: 125 parameter sets; pairwise similarity of rank output between parameter sets (Eqs 17-18, rank-based distance normalized across multiplex networks), PCA projection, k-means on first two PCs, comparison of top-5 and top-100 nodes per cluster (p.6-8, Fig. 4).

findings.finding: RWR is generalized to universal multilayer networks by a column-normalized supra-heterogeneous transition matrix, with inter-multiplex jump parameters lambda and restart parameters eta and tau. The normalization is the step the authors describe as previously unsolved beyond two heterogeneous multiplex networks.
findings.location: Results, Eqs 10-16, p.3-4; Introduction p.2 (normalization unsolved for N multiplex networks)
findings.numbers: Parameters delta, lambda, eta, tau; sum of lambda over alpha = 1 for each beta; sum over j of tau_kj = 1

findings.finding: In the gene-disease LOOCV, combining the gene multiplex with the disease monoplex improves ranking over PPI alone and over the gene multiplex alone. Adding the drug multiplex does not further improve performance.
findings.numbers: No numeric values given in text; comparison is by CDF curves

findings.finding: In the airports network, adding the German multiplex (with French-German and British-German bipartites) increases RWR's ability to predict French-British airport associations, unlike the drug addition in the biological network.
findings.numbers: Three networks: French, British, German airport multiplexes

findings.finding: Bipartite overlap explains the difference: only 23% of genes in the gene-disease bipartite network appear in the drug-gene bipartite, and only 5% of diseases appear in the disease-drug bipartite. The airport bipartites show high overlap.
findings.numbers: 23% genes; 5% diseases

findings.finding: Artificially adding transit drug nodes that link existing gene-disease associations raises LOOCV performance drastically, and the same holds for the airport network.
findings.numbers: 1, 2 or 5 transit nodes per gene-disease association (biological); 1, 2 or 5 transit German nodes per French-British association (airports); no performance values in text

findings.finding: Progressively randomizing the enhanced bipartite networks continuously lowers LOOCV performance, down to the level of using only two multiplex networks.
findings.numbers: Randomization runs to completely random bipartite networks; no values in text

works.title: Social Network Analysis: An Approach and Technique for the Study of Information Exchange
works.summary:
Haythornthwaite's article (LISR 18:323-342; the printed header says 1998, and it began as a 1996 ALISE talk) is an expository introduction to social network analysis. It has no data, sample or identification strategy. It defines a relationship by three attributes: content, direction and strength. A tie between two actors bundles all the relationships they maintain. Strength can be kept as a value or cut at a frequency threshold, and the article warns that cutting it at a threshold throws information away. It sets out five principles (cohesion, structural equivalence, prominence, range and brokerage) and the standard measures: density, centralization, cliques, degree, closeness, betweenness and block modelling. Its Figure 3 shows why betweenness can capture brokerage that degree misses. Drawing on Coleman, Katz and Menzel (1966), it separates sources that inform from close ties that legitimate adoption. It also argues that information becomes useful only when someone forwards it.

For Paul's systems this is a vocabulary paper, not evidence. No number in it carries over. Its real use is as a checklist against the graphs as built:
- **Direction.** The R Stage 3 scrape keeps sponsor-to-cosponsor direction. The AUG workbook sorts each edge's keys and `load_network` averages the two directions, so the cascade kernel runs on an undirected graph.
- **Strength.** Edges are valued (original cosponsor 1.0, regular 0.5, scaled by 1/sqrt of the bill's cosponsor count), which fits the article's advice not to cut strength at a threshold.
- **Multiplexity.** A pair that is tied in several channels never gets a stronger tie. Media edges are admitted only for untied pairs on the CU graph, or take the larger of the two weights under the holistic config.
- **Brokerage.** Betweenness exists only inside the retired InfluenceScore. The staffer graph measures diversity across node kinds, not structural holes.

The informing-versus-legitimating split is a loose conceptual parallel to the engine's two-factor kernel: one factor for diffusion, one for pressure. All bearings below are UNVERIFIED single-path readings (DE-062).
works.question: How can social network analysis (SNA) be used to study information exchange, and what does it offer information professionals (for example, librarians and information providers) for assessing and changing information routes and services?
works.method: Narrative review and conceptual synthesis. It sets out SNA principles (relationships, ties, content, direction, strength; egocentric vs whole networks), five network principles (cohesion, structural equivalence, prominence, range, brokerage), and measurement techniques (graph and matrix representation, density, centralization, cliques, degree, closeness, betweenness, block modelling). It then maps these onto five information concepts: needs, exposure, legitimation, routes and opportunities. No estimation is performed.

findings.finding: Relationships are characterized by content, direction and strength, and ties aggregate multiple relationships between a pair.
findings.location: Principles: Relationships and Ties, printed pp. 326-328 (PDF pp. 4-6)
findings.numbers: Three attributes: content, direction, strength

findings.finding: Granovetter's job-search data: information came mostly from weak ties. Strength of weak ties is cited as a challenge to the strong-ties-only view, while later work is said to reaffirm strong ties.
findings.numbers: Over 80% received instrumental job information from occasional or rare contacts; under 17% from frequent contacts

findings.finding: Egocentric networks suit large or ill-bounded populations. Whole-network designs need responses from all members, and that limits feasible size.
findings.location: Egocentric and whole networks, printed pp. 328-329 (PDF pp. 6-7)
findings.numbers: n actors give n(n-1) possible directed ties; n=20 gives 380 links per relationship

findings.finding: East York residents' community ties are maintained through social ties rather than geographic proximity. Typical residents are described by a few close intimate ties and routinely contacted ties.
findings.location: Printed p. 329 (PDF p. 7), citing Wellman et al. (1988)
findings.numbers: At least 4 socially close intimates; at least 3 persons contacted three times a week or more; most have at least 1 close and routinely contacted tie

findings.finding: Five network principles are proposed: cohesion, structural equivalence, prominence, range and brokerage. These are used to explore relational and positional properties of networks.

Roles and groups can be identified empirically from behavior rather than titles. Informal roles emerge: technological gatekeepers are identified by others, and a technology guru's identity can change with the technology.
findings.location: Printed pp. 330-331 (PDF pp. 8-9), citing Allen (1977) and Burkhardt & Brass (1990)

The article surveys degree, closeness and betweenness. The Katz and PageRank choices attributed to Ardekani are not in this article, so the link is only the shared centrality family.

press_hcoi.py takes its method from Malaterre and Lareau (2024), which correlates text profiles. The article's relational view bears on attribute-based grouping, but it does not discuss text profiles, so no direct contradiction is shown.

The article's cohesion and clustering section (density, cliques, clusters, printed pp. 332-333) and its co-membership examples (printed p. 326) are the framework that committee co-membership analysis applies. Porter's content was not checked here.
The article cites Coleman, Katz and Menzel for the inform versus legitimate split (printed p. 337). Box-Steffensmeier offers congressional evidence on cue-taking. Its content was not checked here.

The article says close reciprocated ties carry legitimacy (Coleman et al., printed p. 337), the in-group legitimation mechanism that partisan cue work would test. Bakker's content was not checked here.
The article's content, direction and strength triad (printed pp. 326-328) has no sign dimension, which signed-network methods add.

works.title: A Network-Based Measure of Cosponsorship Influence on Bill Passing in the United States House of Representatives
works.summary:
Sotoudeh, Porter and Krishnagopal (arXiv 2406.19554v2) build a pairwise influence score from House cosponsorship covering the 111th to 115th Congresses (2009 to 2019). Each pair's share of jointly cosponsored bills that passed the House is decayed exponentially (half-lives of 6, 12 or 24 months), summed over co-party members and normalized by party size. A bill's influence is then the mean or the max of its cosponsors' scores at introduction. In every non-overlapping 4-month window, passed bills score higher than failed ones. The max-cosponsor score separates them better than the mean (relative difference 0.248 vs 0.139 at a 6-month half-life). Half-life barely matters (0.248 / 0.223 / 0.203). Eigenvector, closeness and strength centralities computed on the same pass/total matrix barely separate passed from failed bills (0.002 to 0.004). The analysis is descriptive only: no controls, no significance tests and no strata. A bill counts toward its own score, and as the formulas are written, edges can include passage that happens after the scoring month.

For Paul's system there are three points. First, the paper is cited as the source of the CU cosponsor network's edge weights, but the built weights depart from it on nearly every parameter: an additive ×3 success multiplier instead of a pass/total ratio, a per-Congress 0.8 decay (half-life of about 6 years), a 1/sqrt(C) size discount, unequal role weights and no party normalization. Second, the centrality result backs retiring direction-blind centrality from the Influence pillar. It also shows that any check of InfluenceScore against bill passage would be circular, because the edges are already weighted by passage. Third, code comments and brain notes cite the paper for claims it never tests, namely recruitment chains and influence versus cosponsor count. Paul's 6-month half-life note is also a mis-transfer: the paper's decay applies to accruing cosponsorship influence, not to stance salience.
works.question: Does a legislator-influence measure built from House bill cosponsorship, where two members accrue influence when a bill they both cosponsor passes and that influence decays over time, help explain which House bills pass? Does it beat conventional centralities (eigenvector, closeness, strength) as a signal of bill passage? (Sec. 1, pp. 1-2; Sec. 4-5, pp. 5-18)
works.method: 1) Build monthly undirected weighted cosponsorship tensors: A[t,i,j]pass counts bills introduced in month t that include i and j as sponsor/cosponsors and eventually pass the House; A[t,i,j]tot counts all such bills (p. 6). Edges are symmetric; sponsorship and cosponsorship are treated equally (pp. 5-6). 2) Exponential decay with half-life 6, 12 or 24 months (k = ln(0.5)/half-life), cumulated monthly: C[t,i,j] = sum over n<=t of e^{k(t-n)} A[n,i,j] (Eq. 1-2, pp. 7-8). 3) Party-normalized influence: P[t,i]Dems and P[t,i]Reps are the decayed pass/total ratio summed over co-party members divided by party size (Eq. 3, p. 8). I[t,i] = P_Dems + P_Reps (Eq. 4, p. 8). 4) Bill influence at introduction month t_k: mean or max of I[t_k,i] over cosponsors C_k (Eq. 5, p. 10). 5) Compare passed vs failed bills in non-overlapping 4-month windows via relative difference = (mean passed minus mean failed) / mean failed (pp. 11, 13). Comparators: eigenvector centrality of D = C_pass / C_tot on the largest connected component, eigenproblem D x = lambda x (Eq. 6-7, pp. 15-16); closeness and strength centrality on the same LCC, Appendix A (Eq. 8-9, p. 18). Analysis is descriptive: plots, means and standard errors. No regression, no controls, no formal significance test is reported.

findings.finding: Passed bills have larger bill-level influence than failed bills in every 4-month period from 2009 to 2019, for both mean and max aggregation.
findings.numbers: Consistent separation in all 4-month windows; no per-window counts given.

findings.finding: Max-cosponsor influence separates passed and failed bills more than mean-cosponsor influence.
findings.numbers: Mean relative difference at 6-month half-life: 0.248 (max) vs 0.139 (mean).

findings.finding: The max-vs-mean separation holds at longer half-lives.
findings.numbers: 12-month half-life: 0.223 (max) vs 0.122 (mean). 24-month half-life: 0.203 (max) vs 0.109 (mean).

findings.finding: Half-life choice between 6 and 24 months barely changes discrimination; shorter decay gives slightly larger separation.
findings.numbers: Max-influence relative differences 0.248 / 0.223 / 0.203 for 6 / 12 / 24 months; standard errors 0.0139 / 0.0119 / 0.0107.

findings.numbers: Mean relative difference 0.004 (mean eigenvector) and 0.002 (max eigenvector), vs 0.139 and 0.248 for influence.

findings.finding: Closeness and strength centrality are also weak indicators, and the authors attribute the failure to dense networks (untested).

works.title: Inferring social networks from unstructured text data: A proof of concept detection of hidden communities of interest
works.summary:
Malaterre and Lareau (Data & Policy 6, e5, 2024) is a proof of concept for finding "hidden communities of interest" (HCoIs) when no tie data exist. They fit a 25-topic LDA to 16,917 philosophy-of-science articles (1930-2017). They average each author's topic shares within each of four roughly 21-year periods. Authors with more than 2 weighted publications are kept, which leaves at most 8,009 authors. Authors are linked when the Pearson correlation of their profiles is at least 0.6, and Louvain then finds communities. Communities in adjacent periods are matched by Hellinger distance to trace their history. Over time, modularity rises (0.427 to 0.834), density falls (0.167 to 0.030), and the number of communities goes from 4 to 13. The only validation is that the results agree with the known history of the field. The authors also say plainly that HCoI ties are mediated by text and are a heuristic for possible real ties, not social ties. They argue the method suits policy text but do not test it on any.

For Paul's systems this paper is not new: it is the stated source of fec/network/press_hcoi.py, built on 2026-07-01. That script copies the pipeline almost step for step, except that it uses 19 regex-tagged CU press categories in place of LDA topics. Two system findings back the authors' own caveat. First, the HCoI layer was null for stance co-movement (49%). Second, it recovered only 4 of 41 cosponsor-isolated members. The paper therefore supports building the layer, but it does not support reading HCoIs as coalitions, as closeness, or as influence channels. Those are the readings the system's assumption text, Paul's annotation, and the holistic edge admission lean toward. Everything here is a single-agent reading and is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
works.question: Can communities of actors who share similar semantic content ("hidden communities of interest", HCoIs) be recovered from the texts those actors produce when relational (social tie) data are absent, and can their evolution over time be traced as community genealogies?
works.method: 1) Latent Dirichlet allocation (Blei et al. 2003; Griffiths and Steyvers 2004) on full articles via Gensim, k = 25 topics. k chosen as a compromise between Cv coherence (Roder et al. 2015) over k = 5-100 and manual inspection of top words; k above 35 gave no coherence gain (p.6, Fig. 3). Topics labelled manually into groups A-H (p.7-8, Table 2). 2) Each article's topic distribution is averaged per author per period, weighted by authorship share, giving author topic profiles (p.9). 3) Pearson correlations between author profiles within each period; correlation networks built in Gephi with default Louvain community detection. Authors with weighted publications above 2 retained; correlation threshold 0.6 (p.9). 4) Community topic profile = average of member author profiles (p.9). 5) Hellinger distances between community profiles across adjacent periods; closest pairings used for genealogies (p.9, p.13-14, Fig. 9). works.title: Computational and Graph-Theoretic Analysis of Legislative Networks: New Zealand's Mental Health Act as a Case Study
works.summary:
Ardekani et al. build a citation network of New Zealand Acts. It is seeded on the Mental Health Act 1992 and grows breadth-first for three layers: 27, then 2,159, then 6,021 of 17,709 Acts. Edges are amendment, repeal and citation relations pulled from XML with hand-written regex rules. The rules beat an LLM extractor: precision 0.96 and recall 0.89 in Table 1, against 0.86 and 0.78 averaged over 10 LLM runs. The text gives 93% precision for the rules, which does not match the table.

Nodes are ranked by Katz prestige, which counts incoming paths. The seed Act ranks 2nd in the 2-layer graph and drops out of the top 50 at 3 layers. The authors call it "locally central but not systemically dominant" and say part of the 2-layer rank comes from the seed being the root of its own graph. Louvain finds 14 communities at modularity 0.393 and 15 at 0.392. These communities match committee keyword sets only weakly (Jaccard 0.10-0.67). There are no significance tests, no time dimension, and alpha, the Louvain resolution and the Louvain seed are not reported.

For Paul's systems the paper adds no causal evidence, but it sharpens two methodological points. First, centrality computed on a graph cut to one topic depends on where the cut is made. That bears on the Katz-Bonacich benchmark, which runs on the CU-only kernel, and on comparisons between sector networks. Second, a Louvain partition should come with its modularity and an external alignment check. Press HCoI reports neither. All nodes in the paper are statutes, not legislators. That limits every transfer to Melange's member graphs to the method, not the findings.
works.question: No explicit research question is stated. Stated aim (Sec. 1, p.3-4): (1) build a focal legislative citation network around a seed Act via depth-limited, layer-by-layer expansion, avoiding dominance by global hubs; (2) add LLM-assisted semantic representation of Acts; (3) detect thematic communities and check their alignment with NZ parliamentary committee domains. Scope limited to Acts (historical, repealed, active); court cases excluded (Sec. 1, p.4).
works.method: 1) Rule-based NER and relation extraction on XML Acts using regular expressions triggered by phrases such as "inserted by", "repealed by", "within the meaning of" (Sec. 2.2, p.6-7). An LLM prompt-based extractor was tried and dropped for run-to-run variability and cost. 2) Breadth-first, layer-by-layer expansion from the seed, merging duplicate nodes by title and legislative ID, expanding only newly found nodes, stopping at three layers (Sec. 2.4, p.8-9). 3) Katz prestige centrality by power iteration, x_i = alpha * sum_j A_ji x_j + beta, beta typically 1, alpha < 1/lambda_max; directed graph with all six relation types as edges; rankings reported, not raw scores (Sec. 3, p.12-13). 4) Louvain community detection on 2-layer and 3-layer graphs, modularity reported (Sec. 4.1, p.15). 5) Two LDA topic models per Act: rule-based LDA on full legislative text (TF-IDF, lemmatisation, stopword removal) and LLM-assisted LDA on an LLM summary (max 150 words) plus 10-15 keywords, temperature 0, one pass per Act (Sec. 2.5, p.9-12). Number of topics and priors chosen by coherence score. 6) Jaccard similarity between community LDA keywords and predefined committee keyword sets; each community assigned to its best-matching committee (Sec. 4.2, p.16). 7) Agglomerative clustering merges similar Louvain communities into 6 macro-communities (Table 6, p.17).

findings.finding: Layered subgraph growth: the seed's 1-, 2- and 3-layer neighbourhoods reach 27, 2,159 and 6,021 Acts; 3 layers covers 34% of the corpus.
Authors stop expansion at three layers because the focal Act drops out of the top-50 Katz ranking beyond layer 3.
findings.numbers: Mental Health Act not in top 50 by Katz at layer 3

findings.finding: Rule-based relation extraction outperforms the LLM-based method on both precision and recall.
findings.numbers: Rule-based precision 0.96, recall 0.89. LLM average precision 0.86, recall 0.78. Text gives rule-based overall precision as 93% on 300 sampled relations (p.7), which does not match Table 1.

findings.finding: Mental Health Act is 2nd by Katz prestige in the 2-layer subgraph but falls out of the top 50 in the 3-layer subgraph. Authors read this as local, not systemic, centrality.
findings.numbers: Rank 2 (2-layer) to >50 (3-layer)

findings.finding: Other top-10 Katz movements: Legislation Act 2019 stays 1st; Secondary Legislation Act 2021 3rd to 2nd; Public Service Act 2020 9th to 7th; Criminal Procedure Act 2011 4th to 3rd; Corrections Act 2004 7th to 35th; Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 2003 8th to 37th; Policing Act 2008 10th to 14th.
findings.numbers: Rank pairs as listed (2-layer to 3-layer)

findings.numbers: No measured magnitude given

works.title: The (Financial) Ties That Bind: Social Networks of Intraparty Caucuses
works.summary:
Gaynor builds the member-to-member Leadership PAC (LPAC) donation network for every House member in the 115th Congress (450 nodes, 12,870 directed donation edges) and the 116th Congress (collected partway through the session). Each party is modelled as its own network, because cross-party LPAC giving is almost zero: one cross-party donor in the 115th. Ties are binary and the models are ERGMs. Within each party, members of the same intraparty caucus are more likely to donate to each other. Freedom Caucus is +1.208 and Tea Party +0.686 (Table 2, Model A), and Progressive is +0.381 (Table 3). In the Republican network, members outside a caucus withhold money from Freedom and Tea Party members. Republican leaders give to 86% of members but to only about 30% of Freedom Caucus members (Table 4). Democratic leaders still give to every caucus. Across both parties, vulnerable members (Cook PVI 'likely', October 2018) are about 70-75% more likely to receive a tie, and announced retirees about 40-45% less likely. The design is observational. Weights are ignored, and the text and tables disagree in places: the DW-NOMINATE result in Table 4 versus the p.907 text, and the 116th-Congress replication.

For Paul's systems, this paper describes where money goes. It is not evidence that money moves anyone. It supports Cook PVI as the vulnerability measure that donors act on. It does not support the system's reciprocity claim (D-104..D-108) that a dollar buys more in a competitive seat. Its clearest lesson is structural. Melange treats all co-partisans the same and has no data on the main ideological intraparty caucuses. The scraper's caucus list covers CU-relevant policy caucuses and scores leaders only. The caucus research experiment has membership data for Problem Solvers only. Mentat already holds the FEC leadership-PAC sponsor links needed to rebuild Gaynor's network from bulk data. Any such network would be a donation-tie layer, not a measure of closeness or influence (D-025).
works.question: Do intraparty caucus memberships shape member-to-member Leadership PAC (LPAC) donations in the US House, and how do party leaders' LPAC giving decisions relate to caucus membership?
works.method: Descriptive social network analysis (raw and weighted degree, transitivity; Figures 1-2 Fruchterman-Reingold layouts) on each party separately (pp.895-899). Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGM) estimated with MCMC in the R ergm package (Hunter et al. 2008; Cranmer and Desmarais 2011; Snijders et al. 2006), treating ties as binary and ignoring edge weight (p.899, fn.17). Member-to-member models (Tables 2-3) use four specifications: A both caucus members; B both noncaucus; C donor in caucus, recipient not; D recipient in caucus, donor not; each caucus is entered separately and multi-caucus members get one term per caucus (pp.900-903). Party-leader models (Tables 4-5) are directed ERGMs on leaders' outward ties, with DW-NOMINATE distance from the leader mean (pp.899, 905-907). Mutual reciprocity term included. Only Tables 2-3 are described as undirected analysis (p.900-901).

Aref and Neal partition House signed networks of collaboration and opposition and find three coalitions fit better than party or two blocs. Gaynor finds intraparty faction structure in LPAC ties. Both describe structure below party level. The network basis (cosponsorship or other) is not confirmed from the abstract.
Gaynor cites Porter et al. 2005 (p.893) as prior network analysis of House committee assignments. Her network is built from LPAC money instead.

The Cook 2024 House At-A-Glance lists PVI and ratings for 2024 races. Gaynor's vulnerability is the Cook PVI likely category from Oct 2018, citing Cook and Wasserman 2018 race ratings, not this 2024 product. Code c uses 2026 Cook PVI. Topical link only.

Fouirnaies and Hall use term limits in US state legislatures to show final-term legislators cut visible effort. Gaynor shows peers give about 40 to 45 percent less to retirees, not that they stop. Evidence is state-level, not House. Bears on the 0.60 retiring factor from the other side.

Kim, Stuckatz and Wolters study whether firm campaign donations and lobbying link for the same firm-politician pair and whether donations precede bill lobbying. Gaynor documents a separate member-to-member LPAC channel, which Mentat could capture through sponsor links.

works.title: A network analysis of committees in the U.S. House of Representatives
works.summary:
Porter, Mucha, Newman and Warmbrand (PNAS 2005) build a two-mode network of House members and committees for the 101st-108th Congresses and project it onto committee pairs. Each edge is weighted by a "normalized interlock": the number of shared members divided by the number expected if committees of those sizes were filled at random. Single-linkage clustering then finds about four levels of structure: subcommittees, committees, groups of committees, and the whole House. Subcommittees of the same parent form tight cliques; the Intelligence cluster has interlocks of 14.4-26.6 times chance. A separate rank-2 SVD of the 107th House roll-call matrix (990 votes) splits into a bipartisan axis (45.3% of the sum of squares) and a partisan axis (29.6%). It reproduces 92.7% of individual votes, close to Poole-Rosenthal's Optimal Classification at 92.8%. Committees differ in partisan extremism: Rules is 2nd of the 19 standing committees, Select Homeland Security is 4th of all 113, and Intelligence and its subcommittees are among the 10 least extreme. The analysis is descriptive. No interlock, cluster or the "not random" conclusion has a significance test.

The paper bears on the built system in three places. (1) The committee pillar adds every subcommittee seat on top of the parent seat at one-sixth weight, and Porter shows subcommittee membership largely sits inside the parent committee's membership. (2) In the say-do gate, one recorded Yea on a final-passage vote can corroborate a Champion cell, yet the dominant structure in a roll-call matrix is near-unanimous bipartisan agreement. (3) Two components cite Porter for "community structure", but no code uses committee co-membership or a community partition. Melange has no committee co-membership layer; committees enter only as a scalar pillar. Porter's normalized interlock reweights each edge by size. That must not be carried over to cosponsor edges, because per-edge normalization of cosponsor edges was measured and REJECTED.
works.question: Are U.S. House committee assignments random, or are important committees "stacked" with partisan members? Can network theory applied to committee interlocks (common membership), combined with roll-call SVD, reveal organizational structure and correlations with political positions without using outside political information?
works.method: 1) Build a two-mode Representative-by-committee assignment network. 2) Project onto a one-mode committee network; edge weight = "normalized interlock" = observed common members / expected common members if same-size committees were assigned independently at random from the House. Value 1 = chance, 2 = twice chance, 0 = no overlap. 3) Single-linkage hierarchical clustering on normalized interlocks; dendrogram (Fig. 2) read as levels. 4) Visualization by a variant of Kamada-Kawai spring embedding that uses link strengths (Fig. 1). 5) Voting matrix B (n Representatives x m votes; +1 yea, -1 nay, 0 absent/abstain); SVD gives leading eigenvectors u(k), v(k) and singular values; a rank-2 approximation (Eq. 3) is used. Partisan coordinate = eigenvector that tracks party; bipartisan = eigenvector that groups nearly everyone. 6) Extremism e_i = |p_i - mean p| on the partisan coordinate; committee extremism = mean over members; clusters averaged likewise. 7) Vote-outcome reconstruction: sum the rank-2 approximated votes per vote; positive = pass. 8) Compare individual-vote classification with Poole-Rosenthal Optimal Classification (107th only).

findings.finding: In the 107th House, the four Intelligence subcommittees and their parent committee form a tight clique. Their normalized interlocks fall in 14.4-26.6, far above chance, and the five nodes sit close together in the Fig. 1 layout.

findings.numbers: normalized interlock 14.4-26.6; five nodes

findings.numbers: Rules: normalized interlock 7.4 (2 common members); Legislative and Budget Process Subcommittee: 13.7 (same 2 members)

works.title: Influencing Connected Legislators
works.summary:
Battaglini and Patacchini model two opposed interest groups that bid for votes from legislators who care about money and about voting the same way as their peers. They prove the game has a unique equilibrium. When legislators are office-motivated and have log utility, each group pays each legislator in proportion to that legislator's Bonacich (Katz-Bonacich) centrality. When legislators also care about policy, the weights become a modified Bonacich centrality that depends on preferences and pivot probabilities, and it converges back to plain Bonacich in large chambers. The empirical part fits a spatial-autoregressive model of total PAC money to U.S. House members across the 2004-2012 cycles. Ties come from shared committees (N=2,128 member-Congress rows, phi=0.209, 0.217 after a control-function correction) and shared alma maters (N=1,166, phi=0.084). Degree, closeness and betweenness explain nothing: R^2 stays at 0.148, the same as the model with no network terms. The authors chose not to build the network from cosponsorship, because cosponsorship is itself driven by money (fn. 30). This is an NBER working paper and has not been peer-reviewed.

The most direct bearing is on `fec/engine/kb_benchmark.py`, which cites this paper and implements its prediction as a diagnostic. Its design departs from the paper in three ways:
- It runs Katz on the cosponsorship-based kernel `build_P`, the network the paper avoids because cosponsorship depends on money.
- It pools the Senate with the House, while the paper covers the House only.
- It sets attenuation at 0.85 of the convergence bound, where the paper estimates a weaker spillover of about 0.08 to 0.25.

The stored results (Spearman rho 0.135 against CU money and 0.230 against bank plus financial-services money, n=533 across both chambers, file written 2026-08-18) are therefore unstratified, unverified, and about seven weeks stale. The paper also offers modest support, on a money outcome only, for keeping the degree/betweenness InfluenceScore out of the rank. It also points to a gap: in the allocator, money to one member reaches that member's network neighbours only after a discrete conversion.
works.question: Do legislators' social ties affect how interest groups allocate campaign contributions? Specifically, how do interest groups allocate money across legislators connected by a social network, and do legislators' network positions (Bonacich centrality) predict PAC contributions in the U.S. House?
works.method: Theory: backward induction over a two-stage game (voting stage then influence stage); existence by Brouwer; uniqueness via Lemma 1 (unique voting equilibrium when office-motivated, or policy-motivated with sufficient uncertainty); equilibrium characterized as maximization of weighted monetary utilities (Props 1-2). Empirical: a spatial autoregressive (SAR) model, s = alpha*1 + phi* W s + beta'X + eps (eq. 23), where s is log-transformed contribution-related outcome (eq. 17-18 derive log utility FOC; eq. 20-22 derive the SAR form), estimated by maximum likelihood (Anselin 1988). Benchmarks: OLS without network effects, AIC comparisons, likelihood-ratio test of phi*=0 (chi-square, 1 df), and OLS with degree, betweenness and closeness centrality (Table 4). Robustness: party-weighted committee network, chairmanship-weighted committee network, alumni networks with graduation-period windows (4 and 2 years). Multiple interest groups (Sec 5.2), threshold objectives (Sec 5.3) and heterogeneous policies (Sec 5.4) are extensions that leave the SAR form unchanged up to scale.

findings.finding: Equilibrium exists and is unique in pure strategies under Assumption 1 (noise sufficiently large) and Assumption 2; with office-motivated legislators the optimal transfer allocation maximizes a weighted sum of monetary utilities with weights equal to Bonacich centralities. Under log utility the transfer is proportional to Bonacich centrality.
findings.numbers: Assumption 1: Psi*(beta_max + ...) <= 1/2 (bound on the noise density Psi); Assumption 2: I - 2*Psi*G invertible and positive. Proportionality factor depends on the shadow cost of money.

findings.finding: With policy-motivated legislators the allocation weights become modified Bonacich centralities that depend on preferences and pivot probabilities; they converge to simple Bonacich centralities as the policy-preference weight goes to zero and as the number of legislators grows large.
findings.location: Sec 3.2.2 (eq. 15-16, Prop 2, p. 15); Corollary 1 (p. 15-16); Prop 3 (p. 16); proof in Sec 7.3 (p. 39-40)
findings.numbers: Prop 3: convergence as n goes to infinity; the proof uses Lemma 3.2 (pivot probabilities and their derivatives go to zero).

findings.finding: Committee-network estimate of the network externality parameter is positive and significant; with the control-function correction it is slightly larger.
Alumni-network estimate of the externality parameter is positive and significant.
Network effects significantly improve model fit over OLS without network terms; the likelihood ratio test rejects phi = 0 in both networks.
findings.numbers: Committee: AIC OLS 5686.323 vs MLE 5679.196; LR statistic 11.127. Alumni: AIC OLS 3201.537 vs MLE 3193.922; LR statistic 9.615. Table brackets show p = 0.003 (committee) and p = 0.001 (alumni), while the text says p-value equal to 0.000.

findings.finding: Standard centrality measures (degree, closeness, betweenness) do not explain PAC contributions; the model with them fits no better than the no-network baseline.
findings.numbers: Degree 0.0004 (SE 0.0003) in committee network, -0.0018 (SE 0.0053) in alumni network; Closeness 0.5902 (SE 0.4711) and 0.5903 (SE 0.4771); Betweenness -4.9e-05* (SE 2.9e-05) in committee network, -3.2e-05 (SE 5e-05) in alumni; R^2 = 0.148 across all Table 4 specifications.
