Porter et al. analyse a network whose nodes are committees, linked by common membership (checked in text). B-P build member-level ties from shared committees. Same underlying data, different network object; the rel description of a member co-membership network is corrected here.

Sotoudeh et al. build a cosponsorship-based influence measure and report it is more indicative of bill passage than off-the-shelf centralities (checked in abstract). They do not find cosponsorship centrality weak. B-P avoid cosponsorship as endogenous to money. Together: cosponsorship networks are contested inputs, not a validated influence signal.
Title matches: co-voting network centrality as a measure of political influence (checked; the text file is an online appendix of about 11,000 characters, so the link is verified at title level only).

Checked: budget-constrained influence over networked voters with an opposing controller (shadowing and shielding), so the competing-budgeted-actors framing holds. Calling it the dynamic counterpart of B-P is a characterization, kept as is.

Bonica recovers ideology for candidates and contributors from campaign contributions (checked in abstract). The claim that PACs allocate by competitiveness was not checked in the text; the link is kept as complements on the ideology side only.

works.title: Social network group decision making: Characterization, taxonomy, challenges and future directions from an AI and LLMs perspective
works.summary:
Cao et al. (2025, Information Fusion) is a narrative review plus a descriptive bibliometric map of "social network group decision making" (SNGDM). It reports no new data and fits no model. It defines an SNGDM event as at least three decision-makers whose trust or social network shapes how they reach consensus on alternatives. It classifies the literature along three axes: trust modelling (representation, propagation, decay), internal structure (consensus measurement, power, communities) and consensus mechanisms (feedback, DeGroot or Hegselmann-Krause opinion dynamics, managing manipulation or non-cooperation). It then lists directions for LLMs and multimodal methods. The bibliometric base is 917 Web of Science articles (11,090 raw records, 1,800 after screening; snapshot 25 Sept 2024). Every substantive claim is either a taxonomy label or an agenda item. Nothing is estimated, and the authors say no unified standard exists for evaluating LLM or multimodal SNGDM.

For Paul's systems, this paper is a vocabulary source, not evidence. Three points come close to built components. First, it names multiplicative discount-factor trust propagation and calls decay along chains (path length, node importance) systematically unstudied. That describes the uncalibrated 0.8-per-hop factor and 5-year half-life in the staffer router, and the ASKM product in the recruitment chain. Second, it separates single-path propagation operators from trust aggregation over multiple paths. The member recruitment chain uses only the single most reliable path and says in its own comment that this is a floor. Third, its "pseudoconsensus" warning says high agreement inside a subgroup need not mean agreement between subgroups. That fits the Ward press-lean blocs, which are all labelled pro-CU. Its SNGDM populations are small expert panels with elicited or preset trust, not legislators, staffers or lobbyists, so nothing in it validates any constant. All bearings are weak and UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
works.question: What is social network group decision making (SNGDM), and how should it be defined, characterized and classified? The paper aims to (1) give a formal definition and characterization of the SNGDM framework relative to classical group decision making; (2) map the literature as a taxonomy of trust modeling, internal network structure and consensus mechanisms; and (3) set out challenges and future directions, including how AI, large language models (LLMs) and multimodal fusion could be used. Stated in the Introduction, pp.2-3.
works.method: Narrative review organized as a taxonomy: trust modeling (representation, propagation, evolution), internal structure (consensus measurement, power structure, community structure), and consensus mechanisms (feedback, opinion dynamics, behavior management). Bibliometric step (Section 2.2, p.3): Web of Science Boolean searches on four keyword pairs, manual screening using field and institution shortcuts plus abstract reading, de-duplication. Descriptive outputs only: publications and average citations per year (Fig 2), journals (Fig 3), co-author clusters (Fig 4), keyword co-occurrence (Fig 5). Sections 4 and 5 are agenda-setting arguments with no models fitted or tested. Section 5 covers LLMs and multimodal fusion conceptually; no experiment is run.

findings.finding: Definition 1: an SNGDM event needs at least three decision-makers evaluating alternatives, plus a network among them (nodes, edges, edge weights) that shapes information exchange and the outcome. The authors say SNGDM is more than GDM plus social networks because the two processes are coupled.
findings.location: p.3, Definition 1 and Section 2.1.1 (lines 214-220); coupling claim p.2 (lines 84-86)
findings.numbers: minimum 3 decision-makers

findings.finding: Bibliometric base: four Web of Science keyword pairs returned 11,090 records, manual screening kept 1,800, and de-duplication left 917 articles. The search counts are in Table 1.

Origin: Wu and Chiclana (2014, Knowl.-Based Syst. 59) first presented SNGDM. Papers from the inaugural year have the highest average citations, which the authors read as showing the earliest work is of high academic value. Figure values are not in the text.
findings.numbers: not stated in text

findings.finding: Keyword analysis: current SNGDM research centers on decision-making methods, social network analysis and consensus-reaching processes. The authors call trust behavior a deeper issue that is gaining importance.
findings.numbers: 917 articles in the keyword analysis

findings.finding: Trust representation is classified into four types: binary (trust/distrust), multi-discrete levels, continuous values, and fuzzy-logic values (interval values, intuitionistic fuzzy numbers, trust score spaces).
findings.numbers: 4 representation categories

findings.finding: Trust propagation is characterized by four properties (symmetry, follow-through, directness, divergence). Two approaches are named: propagation operators (six families listed) and trust aggregation over multiple paths.
findings.numbers: 4 properties; 2 approaches; 6 operator families

related.why: A primary SNGDM paper (large-scale group decision making with trust networks and consensus feedback) in the literature this review classifies. It is the concrete method instance behind the review's consensus-mechanism taxonomy.
Most-reliable-path is the single-path multiplicative operator the review lists. Together they frame the choice between single-path and multi-path propagation for the recruitment chain.
Strongest-path search over social tie strength corresponds to the review's trust-propagation operators and path-length decay concern.
Zhou's temporal-graph stance dynamics is the source for the system's neighbour imputation. The review's DeGroot or Hegselmann-Krause framing is the opinion-dynamics theory behind that imputation.
Signed partitioning between subgroups addresses the review's pseudoconsensus concern, that internal homogeneity is not cross-group agreement.

works.title: Predicting Positive and Negative Links in Online Social Networks
works.summary: Leskovec, Huttenlocher and Kleinberg (WWW 2010) ask whether the sign of a hidden directed edge can be predicted from the rest of a signed network, using Epinions (119,217 nodes, 85.0 percent positive), Slashdot (82,144 nodes, 77.4 percent positive) and Wikipedia adminship votes (7,118 users, 78.7 percent positive). A logistic regression on 7 degree features plus 16 signed directed triad counts reaches about 93-94 percent accuracy on a balanced sample of edges with at least 25 common neighbours (Epinions error 6.58 percent versus 14.7 percent for Guha et al.), and the model transfers across sites with little loss. Learned triad coefficients agree with structural balance except for the enemy-of-my-enemy triad, where they match Davis weak balance (no prediction). Status theory explains directed patterns, and a global status ordering satisfies 79-85 percent of edges, well above permuted and rewired baselines. Global balance does not: a two-faction partition scores near the trivial all-positive value (about 0.80) and below degree-preserving rewired networks, so the authors find no significant faction structure. Negative links modestly improve prediction of where positive links exist (for example 0.5612 to 0.5911 on Epinions, chance 0.50). For Melange the sharpest consequence is for the signed mention-layer coalition diagnostic, which compares frustration only against the one-cluster baseline on a substrate that is 83 percent positive by edge count, with no rewired or sign-permuted null and with edge direction discarded. The paper also supports the relationships pilot keeping shared-enemy counts sign-agnostic, and offers a cheap structural consistency check for the LLM-valenced reference edges. All bearings here are new agent analysis and stay UNVERIFIED until reproduced by a second path.
works.question: Can the sign (positive or negative) of a hidden directed link in an online social network be predicted from the signs of the rest of the network? Which local structural principles drive signed-link formation, and do they agree with balance and status theory? Secondary: does knowing negative links help predict positive links, and does global balance (factions) or global status (ordering) appear in these networks?
works.method: Logistic regression over 23 features: 7 degree features (signed in- and out-degrees of u and v, total out-degree of u, total in-degree of v, and embeddedness C(u,v)) plus a 16-dimensional count of directed signed triad types formed by a common neighbor w with u and v. Reduced models: 4-type undirected balance counts, 4-type status counts after canonicalizing signs and directions, and 4-type counts on the all-positive subgraph. Hand-written heuristics (balance majority, status score sigma(x) with predicted sign from sigma(u) versus sigma(v), out-degree majority, in-degree majority) as baselines. Global tests: randomized local search for a two-set partition maximizing satisfied edges (balance), and random pairwise-swap search for a node ordering maximizing satisfied edges (status, as a maximum acyclic subgraph problem), compared with permuted-sign and degree-preserving rewired baselines. Positive-edge existence task: classifier separates true positive edges from matched non-edge pairs with equal embeddedness.

findings.finding: Learned logistic regression predicts edge signs with high accuracy on Epinions, beating the best error reported by Guha et al.
findings.numbers: Error on Epinions: 6.58 percent All23, 6.64 percent 16Triads, 11.45 percent Degree, versus 14.7 percent best in Guha et al. (balanced sample, Em 25)

findings.finding: On the full unbalanced data, random guessing is about 80 percent accurate and the logistic models reach 90-95 percent, roughly 15 points above chance; AUC is consistent with accuracy.
findings.numbers: Balanced sample: AUC about 0.90. Full data: AUC about 0.95; random accuracy about 0.80 on full data, 0.50 on balanced

findings.finding: Triad features gain value as embeddedness rises; degree features are stronger for edges with few common neighbors. Wikipedia accuracy is clearly lower than the other two networks even at high embeddedness.
findings.numbers: Qualitative from Figure 1; accuracy curves plotted for Em = 0, 10, 25 with no table values in the text

findings.finding: The All23 model transfers across networks with little loss: even a model trained on Wikipedia predicts Epinions and Slashdot nearly as well as one trained on the target network.
findings.numbers: Test on Epinions: 0.9342 self-trained, 0.9249 trained on Slashdot, 0.9272 trained on Wikipedia. Test on Wikipedia: 0.8021 self-trained, 0.7722 trained on Epinions, 0.7717 trained on Slashdot

findings.finding: Balance theory matches the learned undirected triad coefficients for every triad type except enemy-of-enemy (mm), where the learned sign agrees with Davis's weak balance (no prediction) rather than balance.
findings.numbers: Undirected model coefficients listed per dataset (e.g., mm type disagrees across Epinions, Slashdot, Wikipedia); weak balance is the Davis 1963 variant

findings.finding: Balance-based models transfer well across domains, while learned status models transfer poorly and often do worse than untrained status baselines.
findings.numbers: BalanceLrn cross-dataset accuracies 0.90-0.92 among Epinions and Slashdot (e.g., 0.9027, 0.9166, 0.9020, 0.9203) versus BalanceDet 0.77-0.84; StatusLrn cross-dataset accuracies range about 0.61-0.83

related.why: Paper does not cite Aref. It bears on the missing null: its global-balance partitions score below degree-preserving rewired networks, the baseline the Aref-Neal diagnostic currently lacks. Item exists in the vault.

Paper does not cite Aref 2020. Both use a frustration-type partition objective; this paper finds no global faction signal in three signed networks, so any partition result on signed data needs a null. Item exists in the vault.
Paper does not cite Zareie. Its Sec 5 shows signed triad features improve positive-edge existence over positive-only path features, not over unsigned similarity baselines. Item exists in the vault.

works.title: Negative Link Prediction in Social Media
works.summary:
Tang, Chang, Aggarwal and Liu (WSDM 2015) ask whether distrust or foe links can be predicted when none are observed, using only positive links and content interactions. They test this on Epinions (14,765 users, 52,704 negative links) and Slashdot (7,275 users, 20,851 negative links). They report three facts. First, negative-link pairs sit close together in the positive network: 82.64% and 87.86% are within 3 hops. Second, signed triads are mostly balanced (92.31% and 93.01%). Third, pairs with negative interactions are far more likely to hold a negative link (t-test p = 5.72e-89 and 1.93e-109). Their SVM, NeLP, adds reliability weights that grow with the interaction count, plus a balance-theory regularizer. Even so, the best F1 on the negative class is only 0.3242 on Epinions and 0.2441 on Slashdot. The simple rule "a negative interaction means a negative link" (negIn) reaches a precision of only 0.2097 and 0.1483. Precision drops the most (-8.70% and -11.08%) when the count-based reliability weights are removed.

For Paul's systems, the paper's main point is a caution. Melange's signed member-reference layer builds negative edges directly from LLM-scored negative references. That is the paper's negIn signal, which the paper shows to be a real but low-precision proxy for an antagonistic relationship. Congress has no explicit foe declaration, so the system cannot score its reference signs against ground truth the way Tang does. Its negative edges should therefore be read as a measure of negative interaction, not of negative ties. The diagnostic signed-coalition partition uses these signs with no evidence-count floor, while the dashboard drawing does use one. The paper's balance statistics support the sign-product logic in the two-hop stance composer. They also give a cheap test the system could run: are negative-reference dyads close together in the cosponsor graph? Every result here comes from 2015-era online trust platforms, not legislatures.
works.question: Can negative (distrust/foe) links be predicted in social media when no negative links are observed, using only positive links and content-centric user interactions (likes/dislikes, ratings, posted opinions)? (Abstract; Sec. 1; Sec. 2, Eq. 1: f: {Gp, A, O} -> Gn.)
works.method: Descriptive analysis (shortest-path distributions, balance and status triad counts, a two-sample t-test and ratio curves), then a supervised classifier, NeLP. Labels: missing pairs are positive samples; negative samples come from pairs with negative interactions (Algorithm 1), refined by status-theory removals and additions, with reliability weights W = f(Nij) if Nij > 0, else r, where f(x) = 1 - 1/log(1+x) (Eq. 2; Sec. 4.1, 5.2). Features: 45 per pair (8 user features for each member, 7 pair features, 22 signed features including 16 weighted triads from Leskovec et al.) (Sec. 4.2). Model: soft-margin SVM with separate costs Cp (positives) and Cn (negatives), per-sample negative weights cj, and a balance-theory Laplacian regularizer weighted by Cb (Eqs. 4-6), solved in dual QP form with a kernel (Eqs. 7-15). Parameters: Cp=1, Cn=0.5, Cb=0.1 (Epinions); Cp=1, Cn=0.7, Cb=0.01 (Slashdot) (Sec. 5.2). Baselines: Random; sPath (predict negative for pairs at a fixed shortest-path length); negIn (predict negative for pairs with negative interactions); negInS (negIn refined by status-theory steps); NeLP-negIn (NeLP trained on negIn labels). Parameterized baselines are reported at their best setting (Sec. 5.2, p. 93).

findings.finding: Negative-link pairs sit close together in the positive network: about 82.64% (Epinions) and 87.86% (Slashdot) are within 3 hops; over 45% have shortest path below 3 and over 80% below 4.
findings.numbers: 82.64% (Epinions), 87.86% (Slashdot) within 3 hops

findings.finding: Triads are mostly balanced and satisfy status theory, supporting both theories as structural constraints.
findings.numbers: Balanced triads: 92.31% (Epinions), 93.01% (Slashdot). Status-consistent triads: 94.73% (Epinions), 93.38% (Slashdot)

findings.finding: Pairs with negative interactions are much more likely to have a negative link than randomly matched pairs; the t-test rejects H0 at alpha=0.01. The ratio of negative-link pairs rises with the number of negative interactions K.
findings.numbers: p = 5.72e-89 (Epinions), p = 1.93e-109 (Slashdot); random-pair negative-link ratio 2.4177e-04 (Epinions), 3.9402e-04 (Slashdot)

findings.finding: NeLP is best on both sites. Random and sPath are near zero; negIn is a strong heuristic; negInS and NeLP-negIn improve on it; full NeLP is top on F1 and precision.
Status-theory refinement (negInS over negIn) gives a small relative F1 gain on both sites.
findings.numbers: +2.37% relative F1 (Epinions), +1.45% (Slashdot)

findings.finding: A classifier trained on one site transfers to the other with little loss, so the features are site-general.
findings.numbers: Figure values not extractable; text says the decrease is 'remarkably little' in both directions

related.why: Title confirmed as Predicting Positive and Negative Links in Online Social Networks (2010). Tang uses Leskovec et al.'s 16 weighted signed-triad features as part of its 45-feature set (Sec. 4.2).

Title confirmed as hidden coalitions in the US House by optimally partitioning signed networks under generalized balance (2021). That is the method signed_coalitions.py implements, and Tang's balance and noisy-label results bear on it.

Title confirmed as detecting coalitions by optimally partitioning signed networks of political collaboration (2020). It applies the same frustration-minimization approach that Tang's balance evidence supports, with the same caution about interaction-derived signs.

Title confirmed as similarity-based link prediction using latent relationships (2020), which predicts positive links. Tang's features include Jaccard coefficients, but its classifier is an SVM and it targets negative links, so same-method overstates the overlap.

works.summary:
Ringe, Victor and Gross (BJPS 2013) ask whether legislators' social ties with allies and adversaries relate to how they vote. Their argument is that legislators treat colleagues as sources of cues. A tie to an adversary is useful when the two disagree, because a predictable opponent gives a reliable signal for confirming or revising one's own position.

The data come from staff-reported contacts among the 65 offices on the European Parliament's Environment Committee. The survey ran in 2007 and 32 of the 65 offices responded (47%). Votes are 40 final roll calls on committee bills from 2004 to 2008. The authors model the dyadic co-voting rate with OLS, with a linear mixed model that has crossed random effects for respondent and alter, and with a log-odds mixed model.

For pairs from opposing voting blocs, each extra unit of point connectivity goes with about 10% lower odds of voting together (95% CI 7-13%; n = 1,319 non-unanimous dyads). On the probability scale, predicted co-voting moves from 52% to 44% across ±1 SD of connectivity. Bloc membership dominates (log-odds 2.91), and party adds nothing once bloc is controlled. The allies hypothesis (H2) could not be tested, because 97% of same-bloc dyads always voted together.

The design is cross-sectional and covers one committee in one policy area, with no identification strategy. The authors report that results are sensitive to specification.

The paper matters here for three reasons:
1. Several of Paul's components read a tie, or a cross-party tie, as a positive conduit for alignment. This paper is evidence that contact between opponents is associated with disagreement, not agreement.
2. It supports conditioning network signals on bloc or party, and keeping edge sign. It does not support pooling ties without sign.
3. It shows that dyadic tests need explicit modelling of network dependence, which none of the system's dyad-level checks has.

Every effect here is an association in one EP committee, measured from reported staff contact rather than cosponsorship. It transfers to the US House cosponsorship graph only as a direction to test, not as a calibrated number.
works.question: Do legislators' social ties with political allies and political adversaries affect how they vote? Specifically, does more social connectedness predict more voting agreement between allies, and less agreement between adversaries (the "keep your friends close and enemies closer" logic)? (pp. 601-603, 609-610)
works.method: Dependent variable is the co-voting rate per dyad (share of roll calls where both voted yes or both no). Model 1: OLS on all observations, presented as misspecified for comparison. Model 2: linear mixed-effects model (lmer, REML) with crossed random effects for respondent and alter, using all observations. Model 3: logit-transformed co-voting rate (log-odds) with random effects for respondent and alter, fitted with lmer and a Laplace approximation, dropping unanimous (0% and 100%) dyads. Predictors: same party, same voting bloc (GUE/NGL plus Greens/EFA vs PES, ALDE, UEN and EPP-ED, inferred from voting; four members belong to neither bloc), same nationality, absolute difference in seniority, point connectivity, and point connectivity x same bloc. Robustness: the authors estimated alternative specifications (lagged votes, joint-membership instrument, reverse-causality models) and report that results are sensitive to specification changes (fn. 81, p. 627); the chosen specification is defended as most theoretically consistent.

findings.finding: Hypothesis 1 supported: higher point connectivity between opposing-bloc MEPs predicts less frequent co-voting, and the coefficient is negative and distinguishable from zero in all three specifications, controlling for party and bloc.
findings.numbers: Point connectivity coefficient: OLS -0.0716 (SE 0.0043); linear multilevel -0.0234 (SE 0.0051); log-odds multilevel -0.1020 (SE 0.0307).

findings.finding: Log-odds effect size: a one-unit increase in point connectivity lowers the odds of co-voting by about 10 per cent for non-coalition pairs.
findings.numbers: Drop of 10% in odds (95% CI 7-13%). On the probability scale, moving from -1 SD (0.6) to +1 SD (3.8) connectivity lowers predicted co-voting for non-coalition pairs from 52% to 44%. A one-unit increase around the median (2) lowers it from 50% to 47%.

findings.finding: Baseline: with no social information, opposing-bloc members are predicted to vote together about half the time, which is the empirical mean for such dyads.
findings.numbers: Predicted co-voting about 50% at the empirical mean.

findings.finding: Same-bloc membership strongly predicts co-voting; joint party membership, nationality and seniority difference do not add explanatory power once bloc is controlled.
findings.numbers: Joint bloc membership: OLS 0.3552 (SE 0.0147); linear 0.5590 (SE 0.0135); log-odds 2.9103 (SE 0.0985), i.e., odds roughly 300% higher. Party: 0.0164 / 0.0063 / -0.0953 (none significant). Nationality and seniority: not significant.

findings.finding: Hypothesis 2 (allies co-vote more with more connection) cannot be tested with these data because there is almost no variation among same-coalition dyads.
findings.numbers: Of 594 same-coalition dyads, 574 (97%) voted together 100% of the time on the forty Environment Committee bills.

findings.finding: Co-voting distribution is bimodal: about one-third of all pairs vote together 100% of the time, and the authors therefore drop unanimous observations in the log-odds model.
findings.numbers: 1,920 observations; 594 pairs at 100% co-voting; only five pairs at 0%.

Item title confirmed (hidden coalitions in the US House, 2021). The bloc-not-party and signed-tie parallel is not re-verified against that item text.
Item title confirmed (partisan cue receptivity). The out-party cue claim is not re-verified against that item text; the lt_priming clamp relies on it.
Item title confirmed (cue-taking in Congress, interest-group letters, 2018). Shared cue-taking framing is supported by titles only.

Changed from contradicts. Sotoudeh builds a cosponsorship influence measure on bill passage. This paper questions cosponsorship as a social-tie proxy (p. 604) but does not test that measure, so it is a premise dispute, not a contradiction.
Item title confirmed (positive and negative links). The shared point that tie sign changes what a tie predicts is a framing link only; content not re-verified.

works.title: Mathematical modeling and analysis of a dark money network
works.summary:
Couch, Fox and Everton (2016) take one US dark money network: politically active nonprofits and linked single-member LLCs that pass money between them without disclosing donors. They apply two decision-analysis tools to it. First, they rank the 8 organizations with the highest degree using TOPSIS over eight ORA centrality measures. The authors set the weights themselves through AHP pairwise judgments. Out-degree gets 0.502, total degree 0.145, eigenvector 0.110 and betweenness 0.075, with a consistency ratio of 0.062. Freedom Partners Chamber of Commerce ranks first (closeness coefficient 0.754), and the ranking survives a one-weight-at-a-time sensitivity sweep. Only the top two match the plain out-degree order, and the authors admit the method produced "no significant changes". Second, they model State versus network as a 2x2 game with payoffs from AHP. The State's equalizing mix is about 85% exposure through the press and 15% prosecution or legislation. There is no outcome data, no time window and no validation, and the 10-strategy solution as printed is inconsistent (0.92 + 0.8 is not 1).

For Paul's systems the paper is mainly a caution about scope and method, not evidence. Mentat's PAC transfer graph follows only FEC-reported committee cash, so it cannot see the nonprofit layer this paper maps. The retired cosponsor InfluenceScore has the same shape as the paper's composite: a hand-weighted mix of centralities led by out-degree. Neither the paper nor the system checks such a composite against an outcome. The paper's AHP consistency ratio and one-weight sensitivity sweep are reusable ways to document owner-judgment weights such as the pillar blend. They do not make those weights valid. The game theory section has no counterpart in the system.
works.question: How can social network analysis of a single US dark money network (politically active nonprofits that take unlimited donations without disclosing donors) be made more rigorous by (a) ranking key nodes with a multi-criteria method (AHP/TOPSIS) instead of a subjective choice of centrality measure, and (b) turning the State-versus-network contest into a game with cardinal payoffs so that kinetic (prosecution/legislation) versus non-kinetic (exposure via press) strategy mixes can be solved for (Sections 1-2, 4; abstract).
works.method: Three linked components. (1) AHP criterion weighting over eight SNA measures (out-degree, total degree, eigenvector, betweenness, hub, in-degree, closeness, authority), with out-degree ranked first (weight 0.50199) and authority last (0.03418) (Table 2, Table 4, Section 2). (2) TOPSIS ranking of the 8 organizations on the unscaled ORA values using those weights (Table 5). Sensitivity analysis follows Alinezhad and Amini (Eq. 1): change one weight in 0.1 steps and rescale the others proportionally (Section 3). (3) Game theory on a 2x2 State (non-kinetic A vs kinetic B) by DMN (maintain centralized C vs decentralize D) game. Ordinal ranks 1-4 (Table 6) are converted to cardinal utilities by AHP (Table 7). Solutions use Nash equilibrium, mixed equalizing strategies, prudential (security-level) strategies and Nash arbitration (Feix solver; Fox lottery-alternative approach). A 5-action State vs 2-action DMN extension uses 10 strategies and a nonlinear program (Barron, Equation 2), solved in Maple 15 (Section 4).

findings.finding: Out-degree is weighted most heavily (0.50199), followed by total degree (0.14517) and eigenvector (0.11045); the AHP consistency ratio is 0.062, under the 0.10 threshold.

TOPSIS ranks Freedom Partners Chamber of Commerce first, Center to Protect Patients' Rights second, and Corner Table LLC third. Corner Table has low out-degree (7) but ranks third. TC4 Trust, third in out-degree (38), ranks seventh. Only the top two organizations match the out-degree ranking.
findings.numbers: TOPSIS closeness: 0.7538 (FPCC, out-degree 90), 0.6192 (CPPR, out-degree 78), 0.4909 (Corner Table, out-degree 7), 0.4887 (American Future Fund), 0.4869, 0.4837, 0.4835 (TC4 Trust, out-degree 38), 0.4817

findings.finding: Sensitivity: raising out-degree weight in 0.1 steps until it is no longer the largest weight leaves Freedom Partners Chamber of Commerce ranked first. Raising the lowest weight (closeness) lets Center to Protect Patients' Rights overtake Freedom Partners.
findings.numbers: Figures only; no numeric thresholds given in text

findings.finding: Ordinal game equilibrium is AD (State non-kinetic, DMN decentralize). Cardinal AHP utilities give State values AD 0.480038, BD 0.28523, AC 0.139265, BC 0.095467 (CR 0.02244) and DMN values BC 0.480645, BD 0.290615, AD 0.137848, AC 0.090892 (CR 0.03248).
findings.numbers: State and DMN AHP utilities as listed; Nash equilibrium AD at (0.48, 0.137)

findings.finding: Mixed equalizing strategy for the State is non-kinetic 84.8385% and kinetic 15.1615%. The paper says this replaces the earlier 50/50 recommendation, and the authors conclude that about 85% of effort should go to non-kinetic methods.
findings.location: Section 4 and Section 5, p. 349-351 and p. 352
findings.numbers: 84.8385% non-kinetic; 15.1615% kinetic

findings.finding: Prudential (security-level) strategies: State plays A (non-kinetic) and DMN plays C (centralize) always, with security levels 0.139 for the State and 0.137 for the DMN.
findings.numbers: security levels (0.139, 0.137)

works.title: Emerging Late Adolescent Friendship Networks and Big Five Personality Traits: A Social Network Approach
works.summary:
Selfhout and colleagues followed 205 Dutch psychology freshmen in 10 randomly assigned introduction groups. They collected five monthly waves of friendship nominations, covering about the first 4 months of university, and analysed them with SIENA actor-oriented models. Each group was modelled separately and the results were then pooled by meta-analysis. Over the first three months the networks grew denser and then levelled off: average degree went from 1.71 to 3.64, and transitivity from .33 to .45. The structural terms were large in every group. Reciprocity was 1.73, and the score tests for transitivity and distance-2 ran from 15.7 to 93.4. A model that looks only at pairs would therefore misfit. Traits had small effects on individuals. Extraverts nominated more friends (ego effect .10), agreeable students were nominated more often (alter effect .14), and openness, conscientiousness and neuroticism had no ego or alter effect. Similarity in openness, extraversion and agreeableness had the largest effects (1.45 to 1.55), but they varied across groups: they were significant in 7, 8 and 10 of the 10 groups respectively.

The paper does not touch lobbying, legislators or elections. Its value for Paul's systems is narrow and comes in two parts. First, it shows that personality matters mostly for pairs of people, through how similar they are. A trait level on one person matters much less. Second, it shows how to test similarity: inside a model that also controls for reciprocity and closure, because a raw correlation can mislead. That bears on the persona-homophily null and on the receptivity layer, where every input describes one member. It also bears on the cosponsor forecaster, which has no reciprocity or closure features, and on the stance co-movement test, which is only a pair-level test. Transfer is weak throughout. These are self-rated single-item traits among strangers forming friendships. Legislators meeting lobbyists, or building cosponsorship records over years, are a different setting.
works.question: Which self-rated Big Five traits predict friendship selection among just-acquainted late adolescents, separating selecting friends (ego), being selected as a friend (alter) and selecting similar friends (similarity), while controlling for network structure and sex; and how do friendship networks develop during acquaintanceship (pp. 513-514)?
works.method: Stochastic actor-oriented models for network evolution estimated in SIENA (Snijders 2001; Snijders et al. 2006), run separately for each of 10 groups, then combined by multilevel meta-analysis of parameter estimates (Snijders and Baerveldt 2003) with group-size weighting (pp. 517-521). Network effects: outdegree, reciprocity, transitivity and geodesic distance-2 (GD-2). works.title: Pinpointing the Powerful: Co-voting Network Centrality as a Measure of Political Influence (online appendix)
works.summary:
This is the online appendix to Ringe and Wilson's paper on co-voting centrality. It holds a proof, simulations and descriptive tables from the European Parliament. The authors build a network from pairwise phi correlations of members' binary voting records. They score each member by an absolute-value (sign-blind) centrality: a member followed reliably by allies (positive phi) or reliably opposed by opponents (negative phi) both count toward that member's centrality.

**Proof.** For a single-party legislature, they show the leader's centrality is at least as high as any follower's. The condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1. The inequalities are weak (greater than or equal), although the n-voter text says "greater".

**Simulations.** There were 1,000 networks per complexity class, with 100 legislators and 1,000 voting rounds.
- The absolute-value measure separates the cue-provider from followers and from "majoritarians" (members who usually vote with the majority).
- The traditional signed measure can rank majoritarians above the true cue-provider when a third group follows at 35% (Figure 4).
- The measure correlates highly with closeness and weighted degree (no coefficient reported), but only about 0.25 with betweenness.
- Moderate and complex networks lose structure when converted to voting data.
- The authors say the results are "highly dependent on parameterization".

**Empirical side.** The data cover 897 MEPs with centrality scores (mean .283). The parliamentary term is not stated in the appendix.

**Why it matters here.**
- Melange has one co-voting layer: the signed vote backbone in the Draft Systems R script, plus its party-controlled Option C. That layer found the raw signed backbone was about 95% party, then dropped the negative side. The paper offers a mechanism for the first finding (the signed measure rewards majoritarians) and an argument against the second (negative ties carry cue-provider information).
- The paper also clarifies the June 2026 retirement of cosponsor centrality from the Influence pillar. The paper treats sign-blindness as a property of a leadership measure, not as a flaw. That supports the system's two-axis rule, which keeps influence and alignment as separate axes.
- None of this transfers directly. The evidence is analytic and simulated, with European Parliament data, and it concerns co-voting, not cosponsorship.
works.question: Can network centrality computed from co-voting records (correlations between members' voting records) identify the actual cue-provider or leader in a legislature, and in particular does a proposed absolute-value centrality measure separate cue-providers from followers and majoritarians where the traditional centrality approach cannot? (Inferred from the appendix; the main question is stated in the published article, which is not in this text.)
works.method: Centrality is built from pairwise phi correlations of binary voting records (Table 1 is the 2x2 contingency table underlying phi, lines 331-341). The appendix uses an absolute-value version of this centrality, referred to as the "posterior" measure, which is compared with the traditional (signed) centrality calculation. Analytic method: Hypothesis 1 (leader centrality >= follower centrality) is proved algebraically for a three-voter legislature (leader plus two followers) with follow probabilities q2 and q3 and leader Yes-probability p; the condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1 (lines 319-345). The result is extended to n voters by a term-by-term comparison, arguing that each phi term depends only on p and the relevant follow probabilities, so it is unchanged as voters are added (lines 347-353). Simulation method: Monte Carlo generation of cueing networks in three complexity classes, computing the posterior centrality from simulated voting records and correlating it with betweenness, closeness, and weighted degree (Figure 5); and t-tests of cue-provider centrality against the maximum follower and a majoritarian across rounds of voting (Figure 6). Figures 1-4 show cue-provider centrality as a function of follow probabilities.

findings.finding: Under the assumptions, in a three-voter legislature the leader's centrality is greater than or equal to each follower's centrality; the condition reduces to q2 < 1 and q3 < 1, which hold by inspection.
findings.location: Complete Proof of Leader Centrality, Hypothesis 1 proof (lines 318-345)
findings.numbers: Conditions: q2 < 1 and q3 < 1 (follow probabilities are probabilities).

findings.finding: The three-voter result is extended to n voters for the single-party case: the cue-provider has greater or equal centrality than any follower regardless of exogenous parameter values. The text states 'greater' for n = 4 but the inequalities derived are weak (>=).
findings.numbers: Proof given for 3, 4, and arbitrary n voters.

findings.finding: Posterior absolute-value centrality recovers the true network centralities of simulated cueing networks; it is highly correlated with closeness and weighted degree even in complex networks, and only weakly correlated with betweenness.
findings.numbers: Betweenness correlation about 0.25; closeness and weighted degree described as 'highly correlated' (no coefficient reported); 1000 simulations, 100 legislators, 1000 rounds of voting; 1000 networks per class.

findings.finding: Simple networks are recovered most accurately; moderate and complex networks less so, because network structure is lost when networks are converted to voting data.
findings.numbers: No coefficients reported by class.

findings.finding: Cue-provider centrality is significantly higher than the maximum follower and the majoritarian; significance grows with the number of voting rounds, and is described as comparable to available EP data at 1,000 rounds.
findings.numbers: Three parameterizations (US, Supermajority, EP); t-scores are described as significant but no t-values are given in the text.

findings.finding: With allies and opponents following at 65% and 35%, cue-provider centrality is clearly higher than majoritarians and followers across the 35%-65% range, though the gap is less pronounced than at 80%/20%.
findings.numbers: Parameterization 65%/35% versus 80%/20% in the published article.

works.title: Detecting coalitions by optimally partitioning signed networks of political collaboration
works.summary:
Aref and Neal build one signed network per chamber per Congress (96th to 114th, 1979-2016). Each network comes from a stochastic-degree-sequence (SDSM) backbone of bill cosponsorship: a dyad that cosponsors together significantly more often than the null predicts gets a positive edge, and one that does so significantly less often gets a negative edge. They then solve the two-group frustration-minimization problem exactly. An LP relaxation with triangle constraints gives a lower bound, a party-label warm start gives an upper bound, and a binary program returns the exact frustration index and the optimal partition. Both balance measures are high and rising over the period (the triangle and normalized frustration indices correlate at 0.95 in the House and 0.91 in the Senate), which the authors read as polarization. Exact solves are cheap for the Senate (about 4 s) and expensive for the House (up to about 13.5 h for the 113th Congress, which has 75,771 edges). The larger side of the optimal partition, the controlling coalition, became more partisan over time. In session-level bivariate mediation models (19 sessions per chamber; association, not cause), coalition partisanship partly offsets the House decline in passage rates (indirect beta 0.510). Majority size does not mediate it, and the Senate shows no effect.

For Paul's systems the paper matters mainly for the diagnostic signed-coalition layer. That layer cites the 2021 follow-up, runs a heuristic local search with no lower bound on an LLM-valenced mention graph, and pools both chambers. At its size (520 members, 7,153 edges) the paper's exact binary program looks tractable. That estimate is derived here and is UNVERIFIED. The paper also gives an outside reading of the project's earlier result that a vote SDSM backbone is about 95% party: under structural balance that is expected, not a defect. It does not license the SDSM null as a fix for the network's degree artifact. That would amount to the per-edge volume normalization the project already measured and rejected.
works.question: Can the members of internally cohesive, mutually antagonistic coalitions in a signed network of legislators be identified exactly by optimally partitioning the network to minimize frustration? And does the partisan composition of the largest such coalition explain changes in legislative effectiveness (bill passage) better than party control or party affiliation does?
works.method: Two partial-balance measures on each network: the triangle index T(G) (Eq. 3, trace-based, fraction of positive triangles) and the normalized frustration index F(G) = 1 - 2L(G)/m (Eq. 6), where L(G) is the frustration index, i.e. the minimum number of intra-group negative plus inter-group positive edges over all two-group partitions (Eqs. 4-5). Exact computation uses (a) a continuous LP relaxation with triangle inequality constraints (Eq. 7) to give a lower bound Y*, solved in Gurobi 8.0; (b) a warm start that initializes each node's group from party affiliation, which also gives an upper bound; and (c) a binary linear program (Eq. 8, XOR-style frustration variables with the lower bound added as a constraint) that returns the exact frustration index and the optimal partition X*. The larger side of X* is the controlling coalition, and coalition partisanship is the fraction of its non-independent members who belong to its dominant party. Inference is cross-sectional, session by session. Two models: a commonsense model (party control = absolute difference between Republican and Democratic seat counts) and a coalition model (coalition partisanship). Each is estimated as a structural equation mediation model with time as the predictor and passage rate as the outcome, using bivariate regressions and standardized betas (unstandardized percentage-point slopes reported for context).

findings.finding: Triangle index and normalized frustration index both show high partial balance that rose over 1979-2016 in both chambers, read as increasing polarization. The two measures are highly correlated.
findings.numbers: Correlation of T(G) and F(G) is 0.95 for the House and 0.91 for the Senate (as printed, 'respectively for House and Senate').

findings.finding: Exact frustration index and optimal partition are computable for dense House networks, but the cost is large. The Senate is cheap.
findings.numbers: 113th House: LP bound (Eq. 7) takes 5,300 s with 28,486,271 constraints; binary model (Eq. 8) has n+m = 76,218 binary variables and 2m+1 = 151,543 constraints and takes 43,523 s; total 48,823 s (about 13.5 h), the longest House instance. House average 17,763 s (SD 15,411 s). Senate average 4 s (SD 6 s).

findings.finding: Controlling coalitions (largest side of the optimal partition) became more partisan (more homogeneous) over 1979-2016 in both chambers.
findings.location: Results, Partial balance and optimal partitioning (p.6), Fig. 3
findings.numbers: No regression coefficient reported in the text for this descriptive trend; Fig. 3 shows counts of the two main parties in the controlling coalition.

findings.finding: Bill passage rates declined over time in both chambers.
findings.location: Results, Mediation in bill passage (p.6), Fig. 5(A)
findings.numbers: House: -0.11 percentage points per session (standardized beta = -0.528, p < 0.05). Senate: -0.35 percentage points per session (beta = -0.852, p < 0.01).

findings.finding: The commonsense explanation fails: party control (absolute majority size) does not mediate the time-passage relation in either chamber.
findings.numbers: No significant mediation reported; text says party control does not mediate the relationship between time and passage rate.

findings.finding: In the House, coalition partisanship mediates the decline in passage rates. Greater partisan homogeneity of the controlling coalition is a protective factor, so the decline would have been worse without it.
findings.numbers: Time to coalition partisanship: beta = 0.771, p < 0.01. Coalition partisanship to passage: beta = 0.661, p < 0.05. Indirect effect of time on passage via coalition partisanship: beta = 0.510, p < 0.05. Direct effect: beta = -1.038, p < 0.01 (as printed; a standardized beta above 1 in magnitude is unusual, so verify against Fig. 5(C)).

works.title: Strategic identity signaling in heterogeneous networks
works.summary: van der Does, Galesic, Dunivin and Smaldino (PNAS 2022, 119(10) e2117898119) test covert signaling theory: people send identity signals that the ingroup reads but the outgroup cannot, and do so more when the audience is mostly outgroup. They built a tweet set of covert and overt left and right messages from rater gaps (1,992 MTurk raters; tweets from 2020), then ran a randomized 8-round experiment (n = 481 analysed) that varied outgroup size (1 to 9 of 10) and the cost of dislikes. With cross-partisan audiences, going from 1 to 9 outgroup members raised covert sharing (AME 0.73, 95 percent CI 0.47 to 0.99) and cut total sharing (AME -5.38). Copartisan audiences showed no effect (BF01 = 43.15), and the cost manipulation did little (BF01 = 16.83). A calibrated payoff model (R = 0.8, r_I = 0.6, r_o = 0.5) puts the covert advantage only at high outgroup share. The authors warn that automated political-speech classifiers probably catch only overt speech. For Paul's systems, the paper bears on the stance and press layers, not the network. Members facing mixed audiences may hedge, go quiet or code their messages, so the press pillar and the DEBATE stance reader could understate them. The say-do gate only lowers tiers, so it cannot correct for members who act more than they talk. The salience-shock backfire term ignores audience composition. Every transfer is UNVERIFIED (DE-062). The subjects were ordinary partisan Twitter users on a left-right axis, not legislators speaking about a largely bipartisan credit-union agenda. This paper offers nothing on graph edges, weights or reciprocity. An earlier relation pass said the text was blank; that result is stale, because the text file now holds the full paper (78,765 chars).
works.question: Do people strategically switch from overt to covert political identity signals (signals readable by ingroup but obscured from outgroup) depending on the share of outgroup members in their audience and on the cost of being disliked? (p.3, lines 309-314 and 320-323)
works.method: Covertness is measured by rating differences: tweets are marked potentially covert when copartisan raters show a large difference in perceived orientation and affect (five criteria, SI Table S6), moderates give neutral orientation and affect, and far copartisans recognise political content; potentially overt tweets use four criteria (p.9). Selection: about 30 candidates per category, then 20 tweets in each of covert left, covert right, overt left and overt right, chosen by author judgement (p.9). Experiment: between-subject audience type (copartisan vs cross-partisan) and within-subject randomized 8 rounds varying outgroup size (1, 4, 6 or 9 of 10) and cost of dislikes (0.5 or 1 cent) (p.9). Analysis: mixed-effects Poisson models of covert and total tweets shared per round, random intercepts per individual, controls for age, gender, race, education and political group; average predictive margins and average marginal effects via the Spost13 package; Bayes factors for null effects from BIC differences (p.5). Mathematical model: expected payoffs of pure overt and covert strategies, with reception probabilities R, r_I and r_o, calibrated to the experiment, then plotted as a payoff advantage over outgroup share d (p.4, Fig. 4). Rater reliability: multilevel regression with Shapley decomposition of McFadden pseudo-R2 (p.9).
findings: Cross-partisan audiences: moving from 1 to 9 outgroup members raised the number of covert tweets shared, controlling total shared, with AME 0.73, 95 percent CI 0.47 to 0.99 (p.5, Fig. 5B).
Under high cost, moving from 4 to 6 cross-partisan outgroup members gave AME 0.42, 95 percent CI 0.08 to 0.77 (p.5).
Copartisan audiences (moderate vs radical): no effect of outgroup size on covert tweets; Bayes factor for null BF01 = 43.15 (p.5, Fig. 5A).
Cost of dislikes: no strong effect on the outgroup-size relationship; BF01 = 16.83; maximum payout gap only 20 cents (p.5, p.6-7).

Participants shared fewer tweets overall as cross-partisan outgroup size rose: AME -5.38, 95 percent CI -6.04 to -4.72; the authors read this as cutting overt tweets while keeping a few covert ones (p.6, Fig. 5D).

Audience reception: covert tweets were liked less by copartisans and disliked less by cross-partisans than overt tweets, but covert tweets did not eliminate outgroup dislikes (p.3-4, Fig. 3, n = 481).

related.why: Noble and Turner model rally, retreat and backfire when an actor goes public, and the salience-shock component implements that model. This paper adds the audience-composition side of outgroup backlash and shows covert messaging only partly avoids it.
Merkley and Stecula show outgroup backlash to overt partisan elite cues in news. This paper explains why senders facing mixed audiences shift to covert cues to avoid that backlash.

Same medium. Fink builds congressional Twitter interaction ties that feed the social layer. This paper implies the content on those ties is audience-shaped, and that heterogeneous followings yield more covert political tweets.

works.title: A Congressional Twitter network dataset quantifying pairwise probability of influence
works.summary: Fink, Omodt, Zinnecker and Sprint (Data in Brief 50, 2023) publish a directed, weighted Twitter network for the 117th Congress. Tweets were pulled on June 9 2022 (3,200-tweet API cap) for 530 active accounts. The common window is Feb 9 to June 9 2022: 179,974 tweets from 525 accounts, though Sec 2 lists 117,974 tweet IDs. After a 100-tweet floor, 475 members remain as nodes. The edge weight from i to j counts the retweets, quotes, replies and mentions that j makes of i's tweets, all weighted equally, and divides by the number of tweets i issued. The authors call this an empirical probability of influence. They pitch it as heterogeneous transmission probabilities for Independent Cascade or SIR simulations, in place of one arbitrary uniform rate. They also say their Viral Centrality approximates ICM Monte Carlo results, but only the companion Physica A paper shows this; this article does not test it. Limitations: one snapshot, possibly non-stationary rates, and no uncertainty on any edge. For Paul's system the article is a direct method source. press_engagement_layer.py implements Fink's normalization with the source-volume denominator. social_interaction_layer.py cites Fink but divides by the engaging member's own post volume, which is the opposite end of the dyad. It also uses a 25-post floor instead of 100, weights mentions 0.4 and skips quotes and replies. Both layers are mean-symmetrized, which discards Fink's direction. They are then mapped through w = 6p/(1-p) so that the cascade kernel reproduces p before party and receptivity factors. The denominator finding comes from reading the code only and stays UNVERIFIED (DE-062).
works.question: Can a public Twitter dataset quantify empirical pairwise probabilities of influence among members of the 117th US Congress, for use in information diffusion and centrality research? Descriptive data article; no hypothesis is tested.
works.method: Descriptive dataset construction; no statistical model. Tweepy and Twitter /2/users endpoints fetched tweets with referenced_tweets, in_reply_to_user_id and entities parameters (Sec 3, p.4-5). For each ordered pair, retweets, quote tweets, replies and mentions of member i tweets by member j are summed, then divided by the total tweets issued by member i. Viral Centrality code from the companion paper is applied to the network; its ICM-approximation claim is asserted here (p.4), not tested.
findings: 530 active congressional Twitter accounts identified of 535 members; 525 yielded tweets in the window (Sec 3, p.4).
179,974 tweets from 525 accounts in the Feb 9 to June 9 2022 window (Sec 3, p.4); conflicts with 117,974 IDs in Sec 2 (p.3).
475 members with at least 100 window tweets form the final network nodes (Sec 3, p.4).
Network is directed and weighted; each edge is an empirical influence probability from summed interactions over source tweet count (Sec 3, p.4).
Authors contrast with the Higgs dataset (ref 2): no interaction-to-probability synthesis there, and most users tweeted only a few times (Sec 1, p.2). Motivating comparison, not a measured result.
Claim: Viral Centrality approximates ICM Monte Carlo results without extensive simulation (Sec 3, p.4). Supported only by the companion paper; not shown in this article.

works.title: Effectiveness of Connected Legislators
works.summary: Battaglini, Leone Sciabolazza and Patacchini (NBER WP 24442, 2018; a working paper, not peer reviewed) model House members who put effort into lawmaking and gain from the effectiveness of the colleagues they cosponsor with. In equilibrium, a member's Volden-Wiseman Legislative Effectiveness Score (LES) is proportional to a characteristic-weighted Katz-Bonacich centrality of the cosponsorship network. They estimate this by nonlinear least squares on 2,176 member-Congress observations (House, 109th to 113th Congresses). Cosponsorship ties are endogenous, so they correct with a two-step control function that uses shared-alma-mater ties as the instrument (first stage on 945,382 dyads). The spillover parameter phi is 0.44 uncorrected and 0.83 corrected (SE 0.05). The selection term is significant. Betweenness, closeness and eigenvector centrality are each significant in naive OLS, but none is significant after the correction. In a horse race, only the model-derived Katz-Bonacich term survives (phi 0.71). The committee-chair effect shrinks about 18 percent (1.97 to 1.61) once the network enters the model. Network effects are positive at every stage from BILL to LAW and grow at later stages. Cross-party and within-party ties have similar coefficients (0.87 vs 0.83), and the gap is small next to their standard errors. For Paul's systems, the paper is the empirical twin of the 2016 targeting paper behind the diagnostic Katz-Bonacich benchmark. It supports the June decision to retire the direction-blind InfluenceScore blend. It also flags that the live cosponsor graph is used without any endogeneity correction. The system already loads CEL LES data, so a direct replication of this paper's KB-to-LES link is cheap. That replication has not been run, and any such result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.
works.question: Do social connections (cosponsorship ties among members of Congress) causally raise legislative effectiveness, once the endogeneity of those ties is controlled, and does the network effect predicted by the model beat traditional centrality measures?
works.method: Structural model yields equilibrium effectiveness E = [I - phi W]^-1 (beta x + epsilon) style spatial autoregressive system (eqs 5-7). Estimated by nonlinear least squares (NLLS). Endogeneity handled by a two-step Heckman-type control function: first stage dyadic OLS of cosponsorship links on alumni links, covariates and absolute differences; selection term xi built from first-stage residuals and inserted in the outcome equation (eqs 8-10). Standard errors from residual bootstrap with 500 replications resampling structural errors by Congress. Partial F tests for phi = 0. Robustness: committee fixed effects (21 committees), state legislative experience subsample, heterogeneous spillovers (eqs 11-14), within- versus between-party networks (eqs 15-17), outcome split by legislative stage (Table 7).
findings: Theory (Sec 2.2, Proposition 1): unique Nash equilibrium in which effectiveness equals a weighted Katz-Bonacich centrality of the social network, given Assumption 1 (invertibility). With no spillovers the model reduces to the standard characteristics-only model.
Uncorrected NLLS (Table 2, col 2): network spillover phi = 0.4448 (SE 0.0233); partial F test of phi = 0 gives 350.81, reported p below 0.001. Positive and significant, consistent with externalities.

Corrected NLLS (Table 2, col 3, bootstrap SE): phi = 0.8324 (SE 0.0516); selection term xi = -0.4133 (SE 0.0741), significant; partial F = 59.51. Phi rises and stays significant after correction, which the authors read as network endogeneity biasing naive estimates downward for phi and biasing characteristic effects upward.

Committee chair effect (Table 2, Sec 4, p.16-17): OLS 1.9669 (SE 0.1147) versus 1.6107 (SE 0.1545) in the corrected network model, about 18 percent smaller in magnitude. The authors say OLS partly captures network effects.

Traditional centralities (Table 4): OLS betweenness 0.0079, closeness 0.0011 and eigenvector 0.1203 are all significant, but after the correction none is significant (betweenness -0.2599 SE 0.1662; closeness 0.0085 SE 0.0086; eigenvector -0.4122 SE 0.2500).

Horse race (Table 4, last block): when the model term is included with the other centralities, only phi stays significant; reported Phi = 0.7095 (SE 0.0817). Text cites this as Column (8) but the table header lists seven columns, so the column mapping is uncertain.

works.title: The Effects of Congressional Staff Networks in the U.S. House of Representatives
works.summary: Montgomery and Nyhan ask whether House members linked by shared personal staff become alike in legislative effectiveness (Volden-Wiseman LES) and roll-call ideology (CJR ideal points). A tie between two members is the count of senior or policy staffers who worked for both offices in the current or previous two Congresses, row-standardized, over the 105th-111th Congresses (435-446 members per Congress). They fit a Bayesian heteroskedastic spatial autoregressive model per Congress and pool the seven estimates. Senior-staff ties show a small positive LES lag (pooled rho 0.043, 95% CI 0.0095 to 0.096; positive in 5 of 7 Congresses). Adding policy staff weakens it (0.013, CI -0.015 to 0.037). For ideology, senior ties show nothing (-0.003). Senior plus policy ties show a small positive lag (0.028, CI 0.013 to 0.047), but covariates already explain R2 above 0.88. Placebo tests help only partly. Lower-level staff ties give a null LES lag. Future senior ties (CI -0.033 to 0.071) and the lower-level ideology placebo overlap the headline estimates, so homophily is not ruled out. The authors conclude that staff may act as extensions of their members. For Paul's systems the paper is most useful as a comparison for the staffer network. Montgomery's tie is an office-to-office sequence link, which the system already emits as directed office moves and shared_with counts. The system deliberately does not treat that link as a person-to-person edge. In this paper the link carries only a weak signal of similarity, and the signal is partly confounded by homophily. It supports showing these counts as descriptive data. It does not support treating them as transmission channels. All findings are observational and House-only. The window is 1997-2010 and excludes committee staff.
works.question: Do members of Congress who exchange senior or policy staff across offices become more similar in legislative effectiveness and in roll-call ideology than chance or observed covariates would predict? Secondary: do staff ties transmit expertise and positions across legislators, as opposed to homophily in staff hiring?
works.method: Bayesian heteroskedastic spatial autoregressive model with covariates, y = X beta + rho W y + e, with e having variance sigma^2 V (diagonal scalars, Student-t-like errors, r = 4), estimated in Matlab with sar_g (LeSage and Pace 2009) (p.17-18). W is a row-standardized, symmetric count of staff who worked for both members in the current or previous two Congresses (p.18). Separate cross-sectional model per Congress, pooled across Congresses with the Gelman et al. (2004) procedure because W changes over time (p.19). Direct, total and indirect effects from the (I - rho W)^-1 expansion (p.20). Two networks: senior-only ties and senior-plus-policy ties. Controls: seniority, majority party, female, African American, Hispanic, committee chair, subchair, majority and minority leadership, power committee (LES); Democrat, female, race and ethnicity, district presidential vote and its square (ideology). Falsification: placebo ties from lower-level staff and from future senior ties (p.29-30).
findings: Senior-staff ties, LES: pooled rho = 0.043, 95% CI [0.0095, 0.096]; positive in 5 of 7 Congresses but not each reliably above zero (Table 1, p.22-23).
Senior plus policy ties, LES: pooled rho = 0.013, 95% CI [-0.015, 0.037]; authors call it consistent with expectations but not conclusive (Table 2, p.24).
Senior-staff ties, ideology: pooled rho = -0.003, 95% CI [-0.029, 0.020]; no reliable effect on roll-call ideal points (Table 3, p.26).
Senior plus policy ties, ideology: pooled rho = 0.028, 95% CI [0.0129, 0.0465]; reliably positive in the 109th and 110th Congresses per text (Table 4, p.27).
Ideology R2 above 0.88 in every Congress, so the tie effect is small against the covariates (p.27-28).
Committee chair direct effect on LES 1.853, 90% CI [1.376, 2.352]; indirect effect via ties 0.442, 90% CI [0.131, 0.826] (p.24).
